title: Method
eyebrow: What these sources actually do, as opposed to what they appear to do
dek: Everything this archive learned the hard way about reading Istrian registers online — written down so the next person does not have to learn it the same way.
lead: This page exists because most of what went wrong here went wrong in the same way: **a tool answered a question that was not the one being asked**, and answered it confidently. None of what follows is theory. Every item was found by getting something wrong and then finding out.

rows.lab: An index strips the field that would have told you the record is not yours
rows.text:
**A marriage of a Defranceschi to a Catharina, at Bakar, sitting in a set of Bakar Defranceschi records, was read as a Bakar Defranceschi's second marriage.** *[It is a Gologorica man's first one](/corrections/), and the register says so in the entry:* «**ex Gollogorizza**».

**⚠ The index does not carry that phrase.** *It gives two names and a date.* ***The one field that would have stopped the misreading is the one indexing drops*** — *because an index records the people, and what made this record foreign to Bakar was not a person but a place written into the sentence about them.*

**The rule:** *an index entry is a pointer, not a reading.* **Before an indexed record is used to build or dismiss a household, open the image.** *Especially when the record sits in a place-based result set: the surrounding records supply a context the record itself may contradict, and nothing in the index will tell you it does.*

*The cost here was nine days and a published sentence. The gain is that [the entry, read, answered three questions at once](/gologorica-line/#bakar1783) — the date, the groom's patronymic and the bride's father — none of which the index held.*

rows.lab: Read the officiant column for everybody, not for your own surname
rows.text:
**A sweep that looks for one name in a column answers a question about that name and no other** — *and if the column is* **who held an office**, *that is not enough to say who held it.*

*[Three entries in which a Defranceschi signs* «per me Parochum» *produced a published sentence saying he held the cure* ***continuously*** *across the span they bracket](/corrections/). The entries between them had not been read, because they did not carry the surname.* **One of them has a DEPRATO signing as** «Parochum» **three weeks later.**

**⚠ The reading was not the problem.** *Every Franceschi was magnified and checked against the scribe's own hand. ***The error was in the white space between the hits***, *which is where a one-name sweep does all its damage: it produces a row of true sightings and an invitation to join them with a line.*

**The rule:** *when a column is being used to establish* **who held an office, or lived in a house, or kept a book**, *read every row of it in the span, not the rows that match. A list of sightings supports* «he was there on these dates» *and nothing wider —* ***and a gap in a one-name sweep is not evidence of continuity, it is evidence of nothing.***

rows.lab: Before drafting a letter, check the shelf you already own
rows.text:
**The archive wanted an archpriest's forename.** *It had him by office and surname from a 1785 baptism, wrote on [the Grach page](/married-in/) that* «he is named by office and surname only; no forename is given», *reasoned correctly that Krbune's surviving film starts eighteen years too late to hold him, and concluded that the route was* ***a diocesan clergy list at Poreč-Pula*** *— a letter, to an archive, under [a standing hold](/errands/).*

**He was marrying people four kilometres away, and that parish's register is on this family's hard drive.** *[The Gologorica marriage book of 1770–1789](/gologorica-line/#marriage1774) names him in full in 1774, eleven years before the only sighting the archive had.*

**⚠ The reasoning that produced the letter was not sloppy — that is what makes it worth a row.** *Every step was right about the* **book it was looking at**. *The step nobody took was asking whether some* **other** *book, already held, touched the same person.* ***A question about a priest is not a question about his parish's registers; it is a question about everywhere he worked.***

**And the same day, [worklist 216 set this very volume aside](/worklist/)** *as* «on the reel the family holds but **stop too early**» *— true of the question being asked of it, and the reason nobody opened it.* ***A book dismissed for one question is not dismissed.***

**The rule:** *before an errand is drafted, run the name and the question against* `searched.json`, `sources.json` *and the* **frame map** *— and specifically against every volume already in the house that the person could have written in, not only the one that bears their place-name.*

rows.lab: check-story cannot see work you never logged
rows.text:
**Fifty-one frames of a register were read across a day, and the only record was a progress line in a work-list row.** *No* `searched.json` *row existed for it at all.* ***And `check-story.py` reported «every hit points at a page a reader reads» the whole time*** — *because it counts* **logged** *searches with hits, and an unlogged sweep is invisible to it.*

**The green light meant «nothing is logged wrong», not «everything is told».** *A gate can only check what exists.* ***Log the search when it starts, not when it finishes***, *with* `outcome: pending` *and the frames read so far — then the counter has something to hold the work against, and a sweep abandoned halfway leaves a record instead of a silence.*

rows.lab: Piping whose.sh into tail throws away the answer
rows.text:
**This archive's rule for the gate is** «*capture ITS exit status — never grep for* ‘FAIL’», *because* `grep` *exits 0 on finding the word.* ***The same trap swallowed* `whose.sh`.** *The command was* `./scripts/whose.sh | tail -13 && git commit`, *and the exit status of a pipeline is the* **last** *command's —* `tail`, *which always succeeds.* «whose: shared ground is staged and --allow-shared was not given» *printed on screen, the chain continued, and the commit went out unflagged.*

**Run it bare and let it fail:** `./scripts/whose.sh` *on its own line.* ***Any check worth running is worth not piping***, *and that goes for every script in* `scripts/` *whose verdict is its exit code rather than its text.*

rows.lab: A sweep that steps by two is not a sweep
rows.text:
**Opening the 1667–1745 Gračišće book, this archive read frames 944, 946, 948, 950 … and the pages looked continuous** — *1667, 1668, 1669, 1670, each opening following the last.* ***They were not continuous. Every frame is its own opening, and half the book was being skipped.*** *It was caught by stopping to ask why the page numbers rose by two per frame-step-of-two, and then reading one of the skipped frames: M01069955 is pages 14–15, sitting between M01069954 and M01069956 and belonging to neither.*

**A sweep done this way reads plausibly and produces a NIL that is half a nil.** *Nothing looks wrong — the years run in order, the hands match, the entries flow. ***That is what makes it dangerous.*** **Before any sweep is trusted, read two adjacent frames and confirm they are adjacent** — *that the second begins where the first ends. One check at the start costs a minute; skipped without it, every absence the sweep reports is worthless.*

rows.lab: Verify the edit landed before publishing the correction that describes it
rows.text:
**A correction was written saying «the page now says so» — and the page did not.** *The script that was to amend it matched on* `"THIS ARCHIVE HAS TREATED GRA"` *against text that reads* `"This archive has treated Gračišće"`. ***Case. The loop ran, matched nothing, changed nothing, and exited 0.*** *The commit went out claiming a fix that was not in the file, and only a* `git show --stat` *showing one file where two were staged caught it.*

**Two rules, both cheap.** *(1)* **Assert after writing**, *not before:* `assert NEW_TEXT in open(path).read()`. *(2)* ***A silent no-op is the dangerous kind of bug in a text archive***, *because the gate cannot see it — nothing is broken, the claim is simply false. Any script that edits prose must fail loudly when its anchor does not match.*

rows.lab: Grep the FRAME NUMBER, not just the name
rows.text: **After four corrections for republishing work already done, this archive adopted a habit: grep the person's name before writing a finding.** *It then published a fifth —* «NASTAVLJA SE», *the card that ends the Gračišće baptism film — which [errand 35 had already recorded in those words](/errands/), with the continuation reel, its frame range and a drafted letter.* ***The habit did not fire because the finding had no person in it.*** **A frame is an identifier too.** *One grep for* `M01070226` *would have returned the errand in a second.* *Before publishing anything read off a film, search the archive for* **the frame number, the reel number and the register's signature** — *the same way a name is searched. A check that only covers one kind of identifier will keep missing the other kind.*

rows.lab: Do not publish a running total as if it were an answer
rows.text: **One column of one census changed its leading parish three times in a day.** *Krbune on six names from a list that measured something else; Paz at thirty openings; Gračišće at seventy-eight; Gračišće again, decisively, at a hundred and nineteen.* ***Only the last was a finding.*** *The other three were published mid-count, and two of them had to be withdrawn.* **When a count is still running, say so in the sentence — «at seventy-eight of a hundred and nineteen openings» — or do not write the sentence yet.** *A ranking from a partial sweep is worth having on the work list and is not worth putting on a page a reader will quote back.*

rows.lab: A superlative needs a denominator
rows.text: **This archive read a six-name list of people who died at Gologorica as strangers, found two of them from Krbune, and published that Krbune was** «**the place Gologorica's incomers came from — more often than anywhere else**». *A work-list row was redirected on it.* ***The set being counted was six, and it was not a sample of migration at all*** — *it was a sample of* **who happened to die here while a stranger**. *The census's own traffic column, thirty openings of it, names* **Paz five times** *and Krbune not once legibly.* **Before writing «more often than anywhere else», name the set you counted and say how big it is** — *and ask whether that set measures the thing in the sentence.*

rows.lab: A column you logged as unread is a blank in the reading, not in the record
rows.text: **This walk read the left half of eight census openings, wrote in its own search log that the right half was** «**not read**», *and then built four findings and three work-list rows on the gap it had just declared — including* «there was a Defranceschi family within marrying distance that this archive cannot yet name». **The right half carried the printed column** «**Locus ex quo vel ad quem**» *and it named the parish and the house number outright.* ***Silence you created by not looking is not evidence of anything.*** *Before a conclusion rests on something a source does not say, check that the source was read — all of it, to the edge of the opening — and if the log says otherwise, go back first.*

rows.lab: Ask whether it is already here — and this is the second time
rows.text: **On 21 September this archive wrote a note saying that with thirteen hundred people on the books, the first question about a find is whether it is already here.** *On 6 October it announced a marriage inside the surname at Gologorica as new, and raised* **two work-list rows** *to find a woman's origin — when [her origin, her house number and her marriage date had been written into this archive on 30 September](/corrections/), sourced to the very frame the walk had open.* ***A method note that is not run as a check is decoration.*** **The check is three greps and it takes a minute:** *the person's name, the place name, and the source, in* `roster.json`, `searched.json` *and the line data —* **before** *the row is raised, not after it is published.*

rows.lab: A married woman is in the Status Animarum twice
rows.text: **Maria, daughter of Joannes Gasparich, born 14 August 1827 and confirmed 9 July 1834, is in the 1826 census in her father's household — and again, twenty-two pages later and under a different house number, as** «**Maria uxor n. Gasparich**» *in the Petrus Rabar household, with the same birth date and the same confirmation date.* ***One woman, entered twice.*** **So a Status Animarum joins two households without needing a marriage register at all**: find the wife's dates in her husband's entry, then find the same dates on a daughter elsewhere in the book. *Birth date alone is a* **candidate**; *birth* **and** *confirmation is an identification. This is how a* «uxor nata X» *stops being a surname and becomes a parent.*

rows.lab: A book is ordered by the number that was live when it was bound
rows.text: **The 1826 census gives many households two house numbers in one cell and labels neither.** *No amount of staring at the two hands settles which is current — but* ***the order of the pages does***. *Taken down the book the upper figures climb (28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 39, 40 …) while the lower ones are scattered (64, 73, 74, 79, 58, 68).* **A register is bound in the sequence of its own numbering, so the figure it is sorted by is the figure that was live.** *The test costs one pass of the column and needs no palaeography at all. It also says where the sort* **starts** — *here about page 20, because the front of the book is ordered by rank instead.*

rows.lab: Ask a kinship question of the book that records kinship
rows.text: **One question — why a Defranceschi died in the «Deprato» house — was answered wrongly twice in two days, both times from the death register's index.** *First: she was born a Defranceschi and married a Deprato (withdrawn — the register names a married woman by her* **husband's** *surname). Then: there was* «no family connection at all» *(withdrawn — there are two).* ***Neither answer was a misreading of the page. Both were deductions about families from a book that records households and addresses.*** *The* Status Animarum *writes the relationship into the name —* «uxor **nata** Deprato», «**mater** nata Bembo», «Mariana **ex fratre nepos**» — *and settled it in two lines.* **The archive had walked that book six days earlier and asked the other one twice.** *Before reasoning about who was related to whom, name the book in the holdings that states relationships, and go there first.*

rows.lab: A one-year gap against the tree is a date against an arithmetic
rows.text: **This archive held Jacobus de Franceschi born 21 July 1761 and recorded that the tree said 1762, keeping its own because it «came off the register».** *The row's own reasoning was right —* «one year of arithmetic apart, not one of evidence» — *because a record giving* «aged N» *yields a birth year that depends on whether the birthday had passed.* ***It simply did not notice that the arithmetic was its own.*** *The 1826 census gives* «**21 | Julii | 1762**» — *a* **date**. **When this archive and a tree differ by exactly one year on something derived from an age, the tree is as likely to be holding the original date as to be wrong.** *Do not resolve it by preferring the register; resolve it by finding a record that* **states** *a date.*

rows.lab: Name a diocese with its year, the way you name a house with its numbering
rows.text: **Gologorica has been in four dioceses in two hundred years** — Pićan to 1788, Gradisca 1788–91, Trieste–Capodistria 1791–1977, Poreč–Pula since 17 October 1977. *This archive wrote* «Pićan … **diocese of Poreč-Pula**» *on an errand asking about the 1880s* — **the present written over the past**. *A request for anything held at the* **diocesan** *level — dispensations, visitation protocols, ordination files — would have gone to the wrong archive for records that are at Trieste.* **A see is not a fixed attribute of a village.** *It is dated, exactly like a house number, and it is cited with its year or it is not cited.*

rows.lab: An index is a second witness, not a pointer
rows.text: **Gologorica deaths p. 48:** «Petrus Chiuch **ex Castro ⟨—⟩otti fossor**». **The same man in the book's own index:** «Chiuch Petrus **furlanus** ex Castro ⟨—⟩otti fossor». *The word* «furlanus» *is in the index and nowhere in the entry.* **Whoever compiled it was adding what they knew, not copying what they read.** So an index in these books can carry facts the page omits — which means a page read without its index may be read short, and an index entry that disagrees with its page is evidence of two informants, not of one mistake.

rows.lab: House numbers were assigned by walking the village
rows.text: **Twelve Udovicich households at Gologorica sit at houses 64, 65, 66, 67, 69, 74, 75, 77 and 79** — and the Zabran at 46–52 and 59, and the Zajz at 111–115. *That is not the alphabet; the index is sorted by name, not by number.* **A surname holding an unbroken run of house numbers is holding a quarter of the village**, because the numbers were given out by walking it. So a sorted list of house numbers is a *map*, and two families whose numbers interleave were neighbours — a cheap, checkable fact that costs nothing but a sort.

rows.lab: Died in the famine is not died of the famine
rows.text: **Petrus Chiuch is on a page where the entries above and below him read** «Fames», «Fames et debilitas», «Debilitas». *His own cause is* «**Volvolus**» — *a twisted gut, at about 75.* **A count of hunger deaths that swept him in because of where he sat would be wrong by one.** The register declines to blur the two and so must any tally taken from it: the cause column is read for every entry, or the number is an estimate and must say so.

rows.lab: A geocoder that succeeds is more dangerous than one that fails
rows.text:
Three Defranceschi were recorded at **«Broken Hill, New South Wales, Australia»** and sat on this archive's map in **Zambia**. The lookup had not failed. **Kabwe was called Broken Hill until 1966**, so the geocoder found a real town with exactly the right name, returned it with confidence, and the map looked entirely reasonable to anyone who did not already know where those men had gone.

**The cause is one line.** The Atlas builder keys every place on `head(name)` — the part of the string *before the first comma*. So «Broken Hill, New South Wales, Australia» is looked up as **«broken hill»**, «Pag, Zara, Dalmatien, Österreich» as **«pag»**, and «San Lorenzo, Santa Fe» as **«san lorenzo»**. Against a world gazetteer a bare settlement name matches the largest homonym on earth. **In every case the qualifier that would have placed it correctly was already in the record, unread.**

**Eight places were wrong**, and the worst by **18,306 km**. Pag — whose own text says *Dalmatien* — was pinned in the Philippines. Mitchell, Canberra was in South Dakota. Athens, Clarke County, Georgia was in Greece.

**Three lessons, in order of how much they cost.**

**A gazetteer lookup on a bare name is unsafe whenever the source string carries a qualifier.** The fix is to try the *full* string before falling back to the head. That is still not done here, because `head()` is load-bearing for how people attach to places across four builders, and it will be changed deliberately rather than at the end of a long day.

**Until then, a gate under it.** `check:places` refuses any pin more than 300 km from a country named in its own text, and it now runs on every build. It was written in another archive of this estate *because of the first three*, and it immediately found **five more nobody had suspected** — which is the argument for gates over care.

**And a trap inside the fix.** Pinning a place by hand only keeps its people if the pinned name has the **same `head()`** as the string the roster uses: *«Dolo, Venezia»* works, *«Dolo Veneto»* would not. Get that wrong and you get a **correctly-placed pin with nobody on it** — which is worse than the error being fixed, because a wrong pin looks wrong to anyone who knows the geography and **an empty right pin looks perfect**. The counts were checked after every rebuild for exactly that reason. *That is a discipline, not a gate, and it is the next gate worth having.*

rows.lab: A record-level roster cannot be checked at person level, and that is the design working
rows.text:
Three archives in this estate spent an evening trying to design one gate: **refuse when a rebuild drops a place's attached people**, so that a hand-pinned place cannot end up correctly placed with nobody on it. It failed three times, and each failure was a different archive's data model rather than a flaw in the rule.

**Per-place** failed on legitimate drops — merging a duplicate, correcting a roster row, resolving a household all move people about without anything being wrong. **Per-person** failed here, and the numbers say why:

| | |
|---|---|
| roster rows | **1,225** |
| rows with a place | **1,057** (86%) |
| names shared by more than one row | **103 names, covering 378 rows (31%)** |
| placed rows whose name is unique | **706** |

*Maria Defranceschi* is **24 rows**. *Pietro De Franceschi* is 16. *Antonius* is 13 and *Antonio* another 13 beside it — **the same name in two latinisations, deliberately kept apart**, because this roster's own note says *identity here is by record, not by resolved individual*.

**So «unambiguous person» is not a property this archive's data has.** It is a property of a resolution step that has deliberately not been taken. A gate restricted to unambiguous names would have watched 706 rows and reported green while blind to the 378 — **which is exactly the third of the roster where the archive is doing its hardest thinking.** Twenty-four rows called Maria Defranceschi are not a data quality problem. **They are twenty-four undecided questions**, and a check that skipped them would be skipping the work.

**Per-record** failed in a third archive, whose registers carry no place field at all — only place names occurring in prose, matched by substring, which is the technique that put Pag in Mindanao.

**The conclusion is about gates in general and is worth more than the gate would have been.** *A gate is written in whichever archive writes it, and looks correct there.* Each of these three would have passed its own author's tests. **There is no shared unit of attachment across these archives** — one attaches places to people, one to records, one to nothing — so there was never a gate to write, only three local ones wearing a general name.

rows.lab: A number that is typed goes stale the day after
rows.text:
The working notes carried a backlog line: *«161 people with no place · **56 unplaced households** · **55 suppressed charts** to review by hand»*. All three were typed once and never recomputed. Checked on 13 September 2026: **one** household has no place, not 56. And **763** of 1,056 dossiers have no pedigree chart, not 55 — the note was wrong by a factor of fourteen, in the direction that makes the job look done.

This archive has already recorded the same failure on a public page — *«nine parishes»* hand-typed beside a computed 1,151, when the real figure was fourteen — and the lesson written then was **«any figure a page states should be derived, not typed»**. The notes were never held to it.

There is now **`scripts/audit.py`**, and `publish.sh` runs it on every publish: roster and household counts, register rows by status, dossiers without a chart, **places holding accepted records that appear on no lane**, and **towns written in the register under more than one name**. That last check is the one that would have caught **Vitipolis** — it prints *«rijeka: Fiume · Rijeka · Vitipolis»* in three words.

**A build that cannot fail its own audit is not a check.** If the audit script errors, the publish stops.

rows.lab: Three easy wins, and why none was taken
rows.text:
**162 people in this archive have no place.** Broken down, that is **104 from the family tree** — which records no place for them, and which is David's worklist, not a machine's — and **55 from the record index**, plus three strays.

The 55 looked mechanical: match the name to a register row and take its place. Run against the whole register, **exactly three of the fifty-five match a single place**: *Josephus Jelčić* and *Josephus Ruman* to Ližnjan, *Antonio Franceschi* to Almissa.

**None of the three has been applied.** All three are **joins on a name and nothing else** — the precise move this archive has a whole page of corrections about, including a portrait hung on the wrong man and a pedigree spliced at the wrong join. A 2% yield is not worth re-opening that door, and the third is a *Franceschi*, not a *Defranceschi*, which is a different question again.

The useful output was not a fix but a **decomposition**: «162 unplaced» is one number hiding two different problems, of which **104 cannot be solved here at all**. The audit now prints the breakdown, so nobody mistakes it for one backlog.

rows.lab: The correction I nearly published
rows.text:
Re-reading image 561, this archive's published transcription — *«Andrea Palin **q.m Pio**»* — looked wrong. At the zoom where a page can be scanned in one pass it plainly read **«q.m Gio.»**, Giovanni, which is one of the commonest patronymics in the book, where *Pio* is rare. A correction was drafted.

**It was checked first, and it was the correction that was wrong.** At full magnification the letter has a straight stem and a closed bowl at the top — the same **P** as in *Pasqua* and *Pinzan* four rows away — and nothing like the looped **G** of *Giovanni*, *Giacomo* and *Giovanna* on the same page. The published reading is right.

The lesson is the mirror of one already on this page. *«Every candidate has to be re-read at full magnification before it is written down»* was recorded here about **finding** a name. It applies exactly as hard to **unfinding** one. **A correction is a claim, and it needs the same evidence as the claim it corrects** — and the tell was there to be noticed: the reading that felt wrong was the *more common* name, which is what a tired eye supplies.

rows.lab: A frame is two pages, and the left one is off-screen
rows.text:
A day's reading of the Vodnjan death register nearly went into the archive with a hole in it.

Each frame of DGS 005497894 photographs a **two-page opening**, and the viewer opens showing the **right-hand page**. The left page is off-screen, and zooming out does not reveal it — the zoom steps stop before the frame is fully fitted, so what looks like the whole image is not.

It was caught by arithmetic, not by looking. Image 564 ended at entry **135** and image 565 appeared to begin at entry **153**. **Seventeen entries had no frame to live on**, which is impossible — so something was being missed. Panning hard left on 565 found book page **162**, entries 136–152, sitting there unread.

The correction is a habit, not a fix: **on every frame, pan fully left before reading, and check that the first entry number continues the last one.** The entry numbers are a running checksum the register keeps for you, and they are the cheapest verification in this whole project.

It also means **images 562 and 563 are only partly read** — their left-hand pages were never opened, and **entries 96–119, June to August 1831**, are still unread. That is written into the queue rather than quietly left for the next person to trip over.

rows.lab: Search the place, not the name
rows.text:
**FamilySearch's full-text search was tested on 13 September 2026**, after standing at the head of this archive's queue for days as the one question that could make weeks of work unnecessary. The answer is no, and then yes to something else.

**No:** the **Croatian parish registers are not in it.** Searching *Gologorica* returns nothing from Istria. The plan to read the Vodnjan books opening by opening stands exactly as it was.

**Yes:** what *is* in it, at full text, is the **American paper** — naturalisation petitions, declarations of intention, passenger and crew manifests. And that changes the question you can ask. Until now this archive searched for a **surname**. Full text lets you search for **the village**, and get back everyone who was born there whatever they were called.

*«I was born in Gologorica Austria ... on February 21 1886. My race is So. Italian»* — Giovanni Udovicich, petition for citizenship, Brooklyn, 1929. *«visible distinctive marks Slavonian race ... I was born in Italian Gologorica Estra, Austria»* — a woman's declaration of intention at Tacoma, Washington, who had married a Joseph on 12 November 1893. **Neither is a De Franceschi.** Both are from a village of a few hundred people that this family also came out of, and that is the point: the emigration was a **village**, not a surname, and this is the first tool that can see it. Note what the clerks wrote in the race box — *«So. Italian»* for one, *«Slavonian»* for the other, for two people out of the same village.

**The counts, corrected.** An earlier version of this page reported 1,952 results for *Gologorica*. That figure was a **year scraped out of a collection title** by a careless pattern, and it was published under a sentence admitting it looked wrong. The real numbers, counted off the result pages:

**Gologorica 19** · **Ližnjan 2** · **Gračišće** three pages · **Crikvenica** fifteen · **Defranceschi** about **9,900**.

And **Vodnjan returns nothing**, because the Croatian name is younger than every record in the corpus. The town is **Dignano** there — about 12,200 hits, most of them the other Dignano, in Friuli. **Search the name the clerk would have written, not the name on today's map.**

Nineteen is the important number. It is small enough to **read end to end**, which is what makes a village sweep a piece of work rather than a wish.

rows.lab: Find the index the clerks already made
rows.text:
The Corsican archive has **no search box** — every module wants a commune, a date and a record type, and says so. That looks like the same wall as Vodnjan: images, read by eye, thousands of them.

It is not, because of one line in a dropdown. Among the record types sits **TABLE DÉCENNALE** — the **alphabetical ten-yearly index** French civil registration compiled for every commune between 1793 and 1902. **Eleven index pages per commune, read down one letter**, against ten years of acts read line by line.

The general rule: **before reading a series, ask whether its own clerks indexed it.** French *tables décennales*, Italian *indici decennali*, English parish transcripts, Habsburg *Namensverzeichnisse* — where a bureaucracy had to find its own records again, it built a finding aid, and that finding aid is usually filmed alongside the register and ignored.

And the corollary, which is the unhappy half: **Vodnjan has no such thing.** An Austrian *Liber Defunctorum* was never indexed, which is exactly why that death register has to be read image by image and Corsica does not.

rows.lab: Test the cheap lever before starting the expensive campaign
rows.text:
The way to match a project that has read a whole town is to **read a whole town** — for this family that means Vodnjan, and the death register alone is roughly **105 images and 4,600 entries**, at something like fourteen tool operations per image.

Before any of that, one question is worth a single request: **is the text inside these images already machine-readable?** FamilySearch has been extending handwriting recognition across its collections. If the Croatian church books are included, the campaign becomes a query. **It is untested, and it is recorded as a maybe rather than a plan.**

The general rule is worth keeping past this instance. **A route that would take weeks deserves an hour spent looking for a route that takes minutes** — and the looking should happen *before* the first week is spent, not after the third.

rows.lab: Show the record, not a family reconstructed from it
rows.text:
**759 person pages said only «no family is drawn for this name».** True, and useless.

**153 of them turned out to have an indexed entry**, and **289 records across the site name other people on the same page** — a parent, a spouse, a godparent, a witness. That is worth showing, and it is emphatically **not** worth drawing as a family.

So those pages now carry **the record itself**: the person, what the index says happened, where, and everyone else named on the same entry, each linked if this archive knows them. Under it, in the archive's own words: ***this is a record, not a family** — the index names these people on one page and does not say how they are related; a parent, a spouse and a godparent look identical here.*

The distinction is the whole point. **The temptation on a thin page is to promote a co-occurrence into a relationship**, and it is how most bad genealogy is made. Showing the raw entry satisfies the reader's question — *what do you actually have on this person?* — without answering a question the record never answered.

rows.lab: Look in your own files before you look anywhere else
rows.text:
Of the **302 people carrying no year at all**, the largest single recovery came from nowhere new. **25 of them already had a dated entry somewhere in this project's own data** — eighteen in `burials.json`, three in `graves.json`, three in the Gologorica file, one in a household — and it had simply never been copied onto the roster row.

That is the second time in two days. **Twelve more had the year sitting in their own indexed record**, whose id was already on their row; nobody had followed it.

The general shape of the error: this archive grew page by page, each page loading its own data file, and **a fact entered for one page does not travel to another**. Before opening an archive, a film or a login, the cheapest possible search is a sweep of every JSON file in the project for a name and a year. It took one script and it beat every external source tried today.

rows.lab: Never mine your own prose for dates
rows.text:
**302 people in this archive carried no year at all.** Three routes were tried to give them one.

Two worked and are safe: **the person's own indexed record** (12 people) and **a dated entry in a household** (29). Both are a record about that person.

The third was **reading the years out of the archive's own note fields**, and it had to be **abandoned**. Seventy-four notes contain a year; only five yielded an explicit *born* or *died*, and **one of those five was wrong** — a note reading «Giuseppe De Franceschi q.m Pietro and Lucia De Franceschi q.m Pietro, both dead in 1830» was parsed as *Pietro died in 1830*. It was his **children** who died in 1830. He was born around 1730.

The reason is structural and worth stating: **a note in this archive is about relationships, and relationships are described using other people's dates.** «Dead by 1823, when his daughter married» is a sentence about a daughter. **One in five wrong is a catastrophic rate for something applied to hundreds of rows**, and no amount of pattern-tightening fixes a source that is talking about somebody else.

rows.lab: An estimate may reject; it may never confirm
rows.text:
Where a person is a parent in a dated household, a birth year can be **estimated** — twenty-seven years before the first child, in a window from thirty-eight to eighteen years before. **64 people now carry such an estimate.**

It is stored in its own field and **never written into the date columns**, so nothing downstream can mistake it for a record. On a person page it says *estimated, not recorded*, in the same breath as the number.

And it is used **one way only**. It can throw out an absurdity — a household beginning three centuries adrift. It cannot confirm a link, and the page says so. In this pass it rejected **nothing**, which is the honest outcome to report: the estimates agreed with every household they were tested against, and agreement of that kind is worth very little.

rows.lab: The index writes Latin in the genitive, and it doubles your families
rows.text:
Baptism entries name the parents in the **genitive** — *filius **Josephi** Defranceschi et **Mariæ***, *son of Joseph and of Maria*. The indexer transcribes what is written, so the same couple appears as **Josephi × Mariæ** on one child and **Giuseppe × Maria** on the next, and any matching done on the raw strings counts them twice.

Mining the catch for households produced **100** parent-pairs before this was handled and **48** after. The fix has three parts: map the genitive forms to one canonical given name (*Valentini* → Valentino, *Ursulæ* → Orsola, *Joannis* → Giovanni), **collapse doubled letters and the -ich / -ć endings** so *Miccoli* and *Micoli*, *Nascovich* and *Nasković* land together, and match on **first given name plus surname only**, discarding middle names — otherwise *Lucia* and *Lucia Michiela* are two women.

What survives the cleaning still is not proof. Three pairs remain that **might** be one household each and are deliberately left as two.

rows.lab: Before you accept a refusal, check your own URL
rows.text:
A **403** stopped this archive for most of a day, and it was self-inflicted. FamilySearch's Deep Zoom tiles are at `…/dgs:FILM_IMAGE/**image_files**/{level}/{col}_{row}.jpg`; the reader had dropped `image_files` and was requesting a path that does not exist. The security service answered the unknown path with **403 and an Incapsula page**, which reads exactly like a ban.

The correct response to *any* refusal is still to stop — and that was done. But the **first diagnostic** should have been: does `image.xml` still work, and is the tile URL the one the service documents? `image.xml` **was** returning 200 the whole time, which was the clue and was not followed. One well-formed request would have settled it.

**A block and a bug produce the same status code.** Tell them apart before you write either one down.

rows.lab: Screenshots are downscaled — do the arithmetic
rows.text:
The reading canvas is drawn at CSS pixels in a **1194 × 1054** viewport, and the screenshot comes back at **800 × 706** — a **0.67** reduction. Twice today a crop was computed by measuring a feature on the *screenshot* and multiplying straight into image coordinates, and twice it landed on blank paper.

The chain is: screenshot px **÷ 0.67** → canvas px **÷ scale** → image px. Miss the first step and every crop is a third too far up and to the left. The corollary is worth having too: because the whole viewport is squeezed into 800 px, a **bigger canvas yields a sharper screenshot**. Drawing at 1190 wide instead of 1020 is free legibility.

rows.lab: Read the catch before you read the film
rows.text:
On 10 September the plan was to read a hundred images of the Vodnjan death register by eye. The tile server blocked, so the **1,508-row harvest sitting in the project from the day before** was read for parent-pairs instead — and it gave four households the archive did not have, plus two children for households that were already standing.

The lesson is not that the index beats the film; it does not, and the deaths this reading was after are **not in the index at all**. The lesson is about **order**. Reading a register by eye is the most expensive thing this archive does, at roughly one page per minute of attention, and it was about to be spent looking for facts already in hand. **Mine what you have harvested before you open the film**, and go to the film for what the mining could not answer.

rows.lab: When the service says stop, stop — again
rows.text: FamilySearch's tile endpoint returned **403 from Incapsula** on the first request of the session: no CAPTCHA, no retry-after, no negotiation offered. The reading stopped. No user-agent was changed, no pacing was tried, no second route was looked for. This is the **second** time it has happened and the second time nothing was attempted. It is worth writing down twice, because the temptation is strongest exactly when the block lands mid-sentence — the register was open at **image 560** and the next fourteen frames were the ones that mattered. The correct move is still to record where you stopped and why, and wait. It is on the Search Register as **blocked**, with the three deaths it was going to answer named.

rows.lab: The place parameter does not filter
rows.text:
On FamilySearch's persona search, **`q.anyPlace` is a relevance boost, not a filter**. Tested with ten values — Vižinada, Draguč, Dubrovnik, Vodnjan, Rovinj, Gračišće, Kaštelir, Ližnjan, and the controls **«Zzzznowhere»** and **«Atlantis»**. Every single one returned the same total: **3,652**. An unrecognised place is silently ignored and you get the whole set back, with no error.

Vižinada and Draguč return **identical** result sets. `f.recordPlace` is a real filter but rejects plain town names.

**Never count records by place with these parameters.** Any number so derived is a count of however many rows you took off the top of a re-ranked list.

rows.lab: A results count is not a promise
rows.text: FamilySearch's persona search reports **3,652 results** and will hand over roughly **1,800**. Past that offset it does not error, does not warn, and does not stop — it **silently wraps back to page one** and serves the same records again, HTTP 200. Offsets 1,800, 2,600 and 3,600 all returned the identical first page, beginning with the same man, `XQMM-LVSJ`. The practical rule: **page until the first record repeats, then stop and say so.** The catch on The Register is 1,800 raw, 1,508 after de-duplication. It is not 3,652, and the 3,652 must never be quoted as a count of anything retrievable.

rows.lab: Harvest with the record id in hand
rows.text: Every one of the 1,508 rows on The Register carries a live link, because the persona id was written down **at the moment the row was taken**, not looked up afterwards. Going back for the ids later is the expensive version of the same work, and usually it never happens — which is how a register ends up with a source column full of blanks. Record the id as you go, or the reach cannot be audited.

rows.lab: A film can carry more than one parish
rows.text:
The catalogue answers a film-number query with the **first creator on the reel**, and says nothing about the rest. **DGS 005497893** returns «Rimokatolička crkva. Župa Vižinada» — and carries **Vižinada's deaths 1754–1831 *and* Vodnjan's baptisms 1815–1866**.

This archive published a confident correction on the strength of that heading, moving seventy-eight records to the wrong parish, and had to retract it within the hour. **Resolve to the film, then open the catalogue item list.** Never stop at the film heading.

rows.lab: An index blank is not an absence
rows.text:
Thirty-nine Istrian places returned nothing in the eighteen-town sweep — including **Gračišće, Gologorica and Crikvenica**, where this archive holds register entries in its own files.

Those registers are on FamilySearch as **browse-only images that no volunteer has indexed**. The two most important pages this project holds were obtained by writing to an archive, not by searching.

There is a second reason, discovered later: since the place parameter does not filter, a search can only ever see what ranks into the top hundred of a re-ranked list. **A blank is a statement about ranking and indexing, not about a province.**

rows.lab: The best records are in the books nobody has indexed
rows.text:
The Vodnjan **marriage register, 1815–1884**, is indexed nowhere on earth — 286 marriage-query arks were resolved against its film and **not one** is on it.

Read by eye, opening by opening, it produced in two days: **five generations**, three separate households, five women who had married out of the name, a priest, a ploughman, a weaver and a shoemaker — and the parents, grandparents and death-brackets of people the indexed baptism register could only name.

**The unindexed book was worth more than every indexed search this project has run.** That is the single most useful thing on this page.

rows.lab: Read the widows' entries first
rows.text:
A first marriage names the couple. **A widow's remarriage names her parents**, because the clerk has to establish she is free to marry.

The deepest generation this archive reached at Vodnjan — **Gio. Maria De Franceschi *fu Pietro* and Michiela Zambaletta fu Cristoforo**, a couple who appear in no baptism register on any film — came out of their daughter remarrying at forty-nine. If you are scanning a marriage register for depth, **the widows are where it is**.

rows.lab: The patronymic is the only thing worth trusting
rows.text:
Vodnjan produced **four men called Pietro De Franceschi** and **two called Cristoforo**, alive in one small town at the same time. They are told apart by «*di* Giuseppe» against «*q.m* Gio: Maria» — the father's name — and by nothing else.

And the difference between **di** (father living) and **q.m / fu** (father dead) is itself evidence: it brackets **Giuseppe De Franceschi's death to between November 1828 and February 1833**, purely from how his sons are written.

rows.lab: A formula is not a fact about a person
rows.text:
«**De Parochi licentia**» — by the parish priest's licence — appears against Don Stefano De Franceschi at a baptism in 1816 and at a marriage in 1833. This archive read that as his particular standing and published it.

The **very next entry** uses the identical formula of Don Pietro Bradamante. It is the register's standard wording for any deputising priest.

**Before making something of a phrase, look for it against somebody else.**

rows.lab: A claim about an unfinished register is a claim about the part you have read
rows.text:
This archive said, repeatedly, that Don Stefano appeared **nineteen times as a witness and never once as the officiant** — while sixty openings of that book were still shut. On image 213 he marries a couple himself.

The honest form of that sentence was always **«in the entries read so far»**. It costs four words.

rows.lab: Names that will trap you
rows.text:
In this parish, ruled out by eye rather than by string-matching:

· **Franceschich** — a Slavic patronymic out of Buzet. Not this name.
· **Francin** — its own Vodnjan family. Not this name — **but Pietro De Franceschi's first wife was a Francin**, so the two are a household deep in each other and a loose search produces nonsense in both directions.
· **De Marchi, De Maria, De Rocchi, Del Carro** — the register is full of *De* surnames in the same hand.

rows.lab: Check the photograph against something
rows.text:
A hand-tinted portrait was published here for months as **Josip Defranceschi of Crikvenica**, the direct line's only likeness. It is from the **Imotski** branch.

Every register plate on that same page had been checked against Pazin and Ledenice. **The portrait was never checked against anything at all** — it carried a name on a card, and the line had a man of that name.

Two branches' photographs sit in one family collection. So do two branches' pedigrees: the retired 2018 GEDCOM spliced Imotski onto this line too.

rows.lab: Do not let a pipe hide a failure
rows.text:
`npm run build | tail -2` reports the exit status of **`tail`**, not of the build. A broken page went live twice before this was taken seriously.

There is now a publish script that builds without a pipe, checks that every source page produced an output file, and **refuses to commit or push if either fails**.

rows.lab: Check that your own crop is not being cut off
rows.text:
The tile reader used to read these registers draws a canvas and the browser **clips it to the viewport rather than scaling it down**. A crop 906 pixels tall in a pane 728 pixels tall silently loses **the bottom fifth of every page** — with no error and no visible edge.

This was running for several openings of the Vodnjan death register before it was noticed, and the fix is arithmetic: **crop height × scale must be smaller than the pane**. Any page scanned before the fix has to be scanned again.

The general form: **when a tool renders rather than reports, measure what it actually gave you against what you asked for.**

rows.lab: When the service says stop, stop
rows.text:
On 10 September 2026, after two days of reading register images tile by tile, FamilySearch returned **403 — «This request was blocked by our security service»** on both the search API and the image service.

**That is a legitimate answer and it was accepted.** No proxy, no delay-and-retry, no attempt to look like a different client. This archive does not bypass bot protection, and the reason is not only that it would be wrong: **a family archive's only real asset is that its claims can be trusted**, and an archive that cheats a source to get them has nothing.

The practical lesson for anyone reading registers this way: **the tile reader is doing hundreds of requests per opening.** Read in short sessions, cache what you pull, and expect that a service which has given you five generations in two days may reasonably decide that is enough for now.

rows.lab: Croatia has no civil registration before 1946, and that is why
rows.text:
Two collection walks on 15 September 2026 produced the same structural fact from opposite ends, and it should have been written down long ago.

**Hungary introduced civil registration in 1895. Croatia-Slavonia did not.** Under the Nagodba of 1868 it ran its own administration, and it **kept the parish registers as the legal civil record until 1946**.

That single fact explains a great deal that had been treated as separate puzzles:

**Why FamilySearch's Croatian collection is «Church Books»** and not civil registration.
**Why Pazin's own catalogue is parish registers.** The state archive holds what the state had, and before 1946 the state had the church's books.
**Why searching for Croatian civil registration finds nothing** — it was never created, so no amount of looking will turn it up.
**And why Međimurje is the exception.** Its civil registers run from 1895 because Međimurje was administered as part of **Zala county — as Hungary proper, not as Croatia**. The anomaly was never archival. It was a border.

*The general rule behind it:* **what survives is decided by which state was keeping records, not by which country the place is in now.** An archive that files by modern country will lose whatever the previous state filed elsewhere — which is exactly what [this map was doing](/elsewhere/).

rows.lab: A rule kept by hand is a rule nobody has checked
rows.text:
The rule for living people is **name and town, never a date**, and every builder applies it itself rather than trusting the page: [the reconciliation](/live-tree/) writes an empty year for a living person, [the Findmypast sweep](/findmypast/) drops the electoral registers, the Social Security index and the obituary notices before it counts anything. That is the right place for it — a rule enforced where the data is made cannot be forgotten by a page written later.

**But nobody had read the result.** In one day this archive grew a GEDCOM reconciliation, a DNA page, a record sweep and a fourth map layer, and the only thing a reader ever sees is the built HTML.

So `scripts/living-audit.py` reads **the built site, not the sources**: 37 people the archive holds as living, every one of their names, against **1,280 pages**, looking for a four-digit year standing in the same run of text. **It found none.**

Getting to *none* took three narrowings, and each one is a lesson about auditing prose. The menu lists every page title on every page and one of the titles is a person's name, so the audit read only what follows the first heading. **No tag may stand between the name and the year** — without that it flagged a households row where the year belonged to the next person in the next span. And **no sentence may end between them**, because «David Defranceski. The 1584 plaque…» is prose about a plaque.

The one hit left is the search index, where the page title *«1948»* sits beside a name in a lowercased string. A rule that is only ever enforced at the door should be checked at the window once a week.

rows.lab: Find out what the index actually carries before planning around it
rows.text:
A work-list row written on 16 September promised **«thirteen birthplaces»** from the thirteen American naturalisation petitions — because a naturalisation petition names the town, which is true of the **document**.

Four transcripts later: every one says **«Birth place: Italy»**. The index carries the country. The town is on the image.

The plan was wrong by a whole job — eighteen images to read by eye rather than eighteen rows to harvest — and it was wrong in the direction that makes the work look cheap. **Read one record of a set before writing a row about all of them.** The same day's sweep did this right elsewhere: the three Italian parish sets were opened, ten transcripts read, and closed as Neapolitan before anybody planned a campaign on them.

rows.lab: A gate that reads from the evidence back to the person, not from the page outwards
rows.text:
Five gates ran on every build here — links, anchors, living people, the work list, the errand ledger — and on 17 September **all five were green while ninety-two people were being told nothing had been read about them**. Nine because a file of fourteen baptisms read off the Fiume register was consumed by no script at all; eighty-three because a banner tested for a household and an index entry and never looked at the person's own records.

**Every one of those gates asks the same question: is what is on the page well-formed?** A build can answer yes to that and still be dropping, in silence, everything it was handed. The class of fault is invisible from that direction by construction.

So `check:evidence` runs the other way. It starts at each **person-keyed evidence file**, takes every person named in it, opens **the rendered page in `dist`** — not the data that was supposed to produce it — and refuses the build unless that page carries a record or a correction. Where the evidence file carries a date it also refuses a page that claims there is no recorded year.

**It does not touch the charts.** A household chart draws `households.json` as it stands and a pedigree draws the export as given; a date recovered from a register does not silently redraw either, and the page now says so in as many words. The gate's only business is to stop a page claiming nothing has been read when something has.

**It was verified by putting both bugs back.** Removing the loader fails nine and exits 1; restoring the old banner fails eighty-eight and exits 1.

rows.lab: A table can be right about every entry and still be lying about what kind of thing it is
rows.text:
«Say Your Name» carried 415 forms of 60 given names and a sentence about itself: *«reconciled by hand from the forms that actually appear in these registers — not from a dictionary»*. **Checked against the records on 17 September 2026: 130 of the 415 were not in them.** Nothing on the page was *wrong* — Grgur really is the Croatian for Gregorio — but the page was claiming the wrong kind of authority for a third of itself, and the Croatian column, 31 of 48 unattested, was almost entirely a dictionary.

**The instinct to delete them was wrong.** A form this archive has never met is exactly what you need in order to go and meet it: *Gergely* is what to type into a Hungarian index, and the fact that no record here uses it is a statement about this archive, not about Hungary. So the table keeps both and marks them apart — **evidence in plain type, lookup aids in italic with a °** — and `scripts/name-forms-audit.py` decides which is which by looking every form up in the roster, the register, the households, the burials, the headstones and the four FamilySearch harvests. The build refuses if the marking drifts from the records.

**The audit also found the column that was missing.** There was no Hungarian one, in an archive whose own place-strings say **Magyarország** — and sixteen Hungarian forms were already in the records, unrecognised, some of them filed as Italian.

rows.lab: A surname with two spellings is two archives, and a nil in one of them is not a nil
rows.text:
Arolsen was searched on 17 September under **DEFRANCESKI** and gave **79 records**. It was searched on **21 September under DEFRANCESCHI** and gave **38 people and 9 archival units** — and the second set is not a subset of the first. **Anton Rudolf, born 20 January 1890, stands in both**, in *different* units: under -ski where this archive found him, and under -schi in the War Time Card File and in 2.3.3.1.

**The engine is matching strings, not people.** Whoever wrote the card wrote what they heard, and the index preserves the clerk's ear, not the family's spelling. A search that returns nothing under one spelling has established nothing about the other.

**The rule: on any full-text index, spend the extra query.** Run every spelling the name actually takes, and treat the union as the result. And check the opposite failure too — the spaced form *«De Franceschi»* at Arolsen returns **960 people**, because the engine splits the token and matches either half. **One query was too narrow and the other was too wide, and neither of them announced it.**

rows.lab: A finding aid's page number is a reading too, and it can be wrong by a digit
rows.text:
The Svetvinčenat index says **«Marina di Piero Defranceschi, 21 Febraro 1710 — c. 6»**. Carta 6 of that volume is in **1706**. The entry is on **carta 16**, where the leaf runs 5, 6, 10, 21 February 1710 in order and Marina sits under *«21 detto»*.

**The tell was chronological, not palaeographic.** The same index put an August 1709 entry at carta 13 verso and a February 1710 entry at carta 6 — **a later date on an earlier leaf**. In a register kept in order that cannot happen, and it is the cheapest check there is: **sort your citations by date and see whether the page numbers rise with them.**

This is the same lesson the Pazin misread taught in a different costume — *«the cheapest check is whether the sequence you have written down is possible»* — and it is worth stating twice because the two failures look nothing alike. There the ambiguous character was in the record; here it is in the finding aid. **A citation is a claim, and it is the kind of claim that can be tested before it is followed.**

rows.lab: With thirteen hundred people on the books, the first question about a find is whether it is already here
rows.text:
**On 21 September a naturalisation petition came up naming a man born at «Gallignana, Austria» — Gračišće, this archive's own origin parish — who sailed from Trieste on the *Martha Washington* in 1910 and settled in Brooklyn.** It was about to be written up as the find of the day.

**It had been published here for weeks.** He is *Giuseppe Defranceschi, born 1892*, **the first of the Eleven to go**, and [his page](/the-eleven/) already carried the petition, the certificate number, the ship, the date of arrival and his address at **148 Sackett Street**. The only reason it was caught is that the roster was searched before the note was written.

**This is a structural hazard of a one-name study and it gets worse, not better.** The roster passed **1,350 rows** today. Any archive large enough to be useful is large enough that **a genuine document can be genuinely new to the reader and old to the archive** — and the feeling of discovery is identical either way.

**The rule: grep before you publish.** Not the person's name, which is shared by dozens here — a **hard string from the document**: a certificate number, a ship, a street. On the same afternoon that test cleared the Chicago card (*«2336 W. Superior»*, *«151190»* — nothing) and caught Joseph (*«Martha Washington»* — five files).

rows.lab: A pattern that matches a command matches it in every archive on the machine
rows.text:
**For weeks this session ran `pkill -f "astro build"` before every publish, to clear a stuck build of its own. `pkill -f` matches the full command line of every process on the machine — and every archive on this Mac builds with `astro build`.** It was reaping all of them.

**The Lerena session worked it out and said so**, having lost three `verify.sh` runs to it. Checked at that moment, `pgrep -fl "astro build"` showed live builds under **Blazevic** and **D'arcy** as well. **And one of this archive's own publishes had died the same way — exit 144, mid-render — and was written off as an unreproducible fault.**

**The second-order damage is the expensive part.** A SIGTERM'd build inside a gate chain exits non-zero *after* several gates have already printed `ok`, so the failure surfaces as a clean-looking log with an unexplained `EXIT=1`. **It looks exactly like bad data.** That is two sessions hunting a fault in their own work that was never there.

**The fix is `scripts/stop-my-build.sh`**: resolve the repo root and match `pgrep -f "$ROOT/site/node_modules/.bin/astro"` — the absolute project path, which every node build carries in its command line — and kill only those. **The rule behind it: a process pattern is a global selector. Scope it to a path, not to a command.**

rows.lab: A scan that is fast enough to be worth doing is never good enough to be believed
rows.text:
**Reading a parish register page by page costs four calls a frame — render each page, screenshot each page. Cropping both pages into one canvas halves it.** At 880 pixels across an entire opening the hand is still legible enough to *spot* a nine-letter surname, and that is what a sweep needs.

**On the first spread it was used in anger it produced a false positive.** *«Maria Catarina filia legitima **Dominici Dassanich q. Laurentij** et Joanne ejus uxoris»*, carta 82, 16 October 1780 — at spread scale indistinguishable from *Dominici Defranceschi*: the same length, the same ascenders, the same slot in a formula that always runs *filia legitima [father] et [mother] ejus uxoris*. **It was a new child of the name for about a minute.**

**The formula is what makes it dangerous.** Every entry on the page has a long surname in exactly that position, so the eye is not matching a word, it is matching a shape in a slot — and half the parish fits.

**The rule: scan wide, confirm narrow, and never let a candidate cross into a note without a magnified crop of its own.** At Svetvinčenat this surname has at least three near-twins — **Defranzieri** on the index page, **Nadal Venir** four entries below *D. Nadal Defraneschi*, and now **Dassanich** — all three met in a single day.

---

**Amended, after the D'Arcy session found the asymmetry this note had missed.**

This was filed alongside their wildcard as the same fault — an instrument that buys reach by giving up discrimination. **It is not the same, and the difference decides how each may be used.**

**Their dilution is printed in the result set. This one is not.** A wildcard hands back 608 rows with *de France* and *de Franca* **legible in them**, and the wrong ones are discarded by reading the output. **This crop hands back *Dassanich* already converted into *Defranceschi*.** The surname is not in the output to be judged — only the reading of it is. So the discarding can only happen against the original image at full resolution, **which is the step the crop existed to skip**.

**So the saving is smaller than this note first claimed, and it was wrong to call it a halving.** Two calls a frame buys a *shortlist*, not a reading. Every candidate still costs the full-resolution look; the only frames it truly saves are the ones with no candidate at all — which, at four false positives across seven spreads, is most of them but not nearly all.

**The corrected rule: use it to rank which spreads to open, never to confirm what is on one.** And the general form, which is theirs: **both instruments trade discrimination for reach, and neither reports which of the two it is doing.** A safe instrument would state its own selectivity. This one cannot even in principle, because its output has already collapsed the evidence into a judgement.

**And the variable that governs both instruments is not in either of them.**

The frames this crop genuinely saves are the ones with **no** candidate on them. So **the saving is a function of how rare the surname's silhouette is in that parish, not of the crop.** Where the shape is common the crop saves nothing and costs a false positive a frame; where it is rare it saves almost everything.

**That is the same number as the wildcard's dilution** — `defranceschi` returns 5 in England and `defranc*` returns 608, because *Defranc-* is a native English surname stem; in a corpus where it is foreign the same query is clean. **Both instruments are only as good as the rarity of the thing being sought in the corpus they are pointed at, and neither of them knows that number.**

**Which gives the only honest way to use either: measure the rarity first.** One exact-spelling query before the wildcard; one full-resolution spread before the sweep. **The cost of that measurement is one call, and without it neither instrument can tell you whether it is about to save you a day or invent a family.**

rows.lab: A silent narrowing is worse than a silent zero, because it answers
rows.text:
**Findmypast's year filter takes `yearofbirth` and `yearofbirth_offset`, and the offset misbehaves in the one way that cannot be spotted from the result.** Measured on 21 September against a single fixed query — *defrance\**, census and land, Great Britain, born 1855 — varying nothing but the offset:

| offset | results |
|---|---:|
| 0 | **17** |
| 3 | **24** |
| 7 | **45** |
| 40 | **205** |
| **45** | **17** |

**Arbitrary integers are honoured** — the dropdown's 0/1/2/5/10/20/40 are presets, not a whitelist, and 3 and 7 give genuine windows. **But anything above 40 collapses to an exact-year match.** Offset 45 returns precisely the offset-0 count: **the narrowest search there is, wearing the clothes of the widest.**

**This archive was caught by it.** A *Cosulich* query at offset 45 returned a clean zero and was read as «nobody of that name in that window». It had quietly become «born in exactly 1855», and nobody was. The zero was true and meaningless.

**The general form is the point.** A parameter that fails by *erroring* costs a retry. A parameter that fails by *returning nothing* at least looks suspicious. **A parameter that fails by returning a real, small, plausible answer costs a false finding**, because there is nothing in the result to distrust. **Before believing any filtered nil, vary the filter and watch the count move.** If it does not move, the filter was never applied; if it moves the wrong way, it was applied as something else.

rows.lab: Ask of every data file: does anything on earth read it?
rows.text:
**The D'Arcy session found a file in its own archive that nothing read — a register of spelling folds it had examined and *refused*, with reasons beside each.** Its own opening note said refusals get overturned by whoever next runs the tool, and since nothing consulted it, that is exactly what would have happened. Their line for it is the right one: **a refusal nobody consults is not a decision, it is a diary entry.**

**Run here, the audit is one line** — for each `src/data/*.json`, grep the pages, components and scripts for its filename — and it found **one orphan out of sixty-odd files**: `namefold-extra.json`, 578 given-name folds.

**And then the second half of the check mattered more than the first.** The alarming reading was *«five hundred folds built to widen the search box, wired to nothing»*. **It is a strict subset**: all 578 are inside `namefold.json`, which carries 594 and is wired into [the register](/register/). Nothing is missing from the site and no search is narrower than it should be.

**It is kept rather than deleted, for one sentence it contains**: *«JAN is the trap — it is a real given name and it is also how a date writes January, and in the Booyzen archive folding it made 338 of 346 people match a search for JOHN»*, with Zan, Gio, Nane, Ive and Ana beside it. **That is the refusal.** The 578 folds are duplicated elsewhere; the reason six of them were left out is recorded nowhere else. **An orphan file is worth auditing for what it decided, not only for what it holds.**

rows.lab: Ask what the finding aid has already ruled out before reading past it
rows.text:
**A page-by-page read was about to begin over forty-seven frames of Svetvinčenat, 1750 to 1763.** Before it started, one question: *what does the volume's own index already say about those years?*

**It says there is not one child of the name in any of them.** The index holds seven Defranceschi entries and **every one is 1734 or earlier**, in a volume that runs to 1763.

**That is not a reason to skip the read — it is the thing that tells you what the read is for.** The index runs **B to P**, so it is blind to **A** and **R–Z**. If children of the name exist in those twenty-nine years, their forenames are *Antonio, Andrea, Anzolo, Rocco, Simon, Tomaso, Vito, Zuanne* — and the man this archive is hunting, the Antonio of the 1780 exemption, is the first of those.

**The general rule: a finding aid's silence is evidence, but only once you know its extent.** This archive [learned that the hard way last night](/corrections/), when it was about to trust the same index for the same Antonio. Turned round, the same fact becomes a prediction: **the read is no longer looking for a surname, it is looking for eight forenames**, which is a different and far cheaper thing to look for.

rows.lab: A twentieth-century commune has a typed index, and it is not where the handwriting is
rows.text: Thiébauménil's tables décennales for 1873–1932 are catalogued as seventy-three images of a register, which reads like seventy-three pages to squint at. They are nothing of the sort: they were **typed and printed on 27 November 1995** from the commune's own database, alphabetical by surname, one line per act, with the act number and the exact date. **Two screenshots replaced a 312-image sweep of the birth registers.** The rule that came out of it: before opening any French commune's acts, open its TD and look at what century the TD is *from*. A table made in the 1990s is machine-legible where the acts are not, and it indexes the acts either side of the decade boundaries the catalogue advertises. The same volume also answers a negative cleanly — the marriage table for 1903–1912 runs *Humbert → Leybach* with nothing between, which is a much firmer nil than failing to spot a name in a year of handwriting.

rows.lab: The register changed language, and the search term had to change with it
rows.text: Svetvinčenat's marriage register is Italian from 1762 and **Latin from 1770**, in the middle of the same bound volume and with no announcement. Up to image 21 the entries read *«Adì … contrasse il matrimonio per verba de presenti con …»*; from image 22 they read *«Tribus premissis denunciationibus … matrimonio juncti sunt»*. The family name goes with it: **de Franceschi** in the Italian stretch, **Franceschi** after the Latin nominative takes over, and the forename is **Giacobus**, not Giacomo. A page-by-page eye trained on one of those shapes slides straight past the other. **Fix the language at every frame you open, not at the start of the volume** — the tell is the first word of the entry, not the heading, and a volume that was catalogued as one thing is routinely two.

rows.lab: A name that keeps recurring is a job before it is an honour
rows.text: Antonio de Franceschi witnesses six weddings at Svetvinčenat in ten months of 1773. Written up the same afternoon, that read as standing: the parish keeps asking for him. Sixteen frames later the register calls him *«Campanaro»* — the bell-ringer — and the pattern collapses into something much more ordinary: he is in the church because that is where he works. **Before treating a recurrence as significant, look for the office that would produce it anyway** — sexton, bell-ringer, schoolmaster, clerk, innkeeper next door. The tell is usually written down somewhere later in the same volume, in a formula the eye skips because it sits after the name rather than before it. **And when the office turns up, check whether anyone else holds it too**: here Joannes Sain is styled *campanaro* four months after Antonio last is, which killed the tidier sentence — «the bell-ringer of Svetvinčenat» — before it could be published.

rows.lab: Run the neighbouring archive's test before deciding it does not apply to you
rows.text: The D'Arcy study found thirty-six of its map pins sitting on a containing place's coordinate and stamped *exact* — its own subject town shown on the centre of England. It sent the detector over. The cheap response would have been to reason that this archive's map is built differently and move on. **Porting the test cost twenty lines and found four**, and — this is the part worth keeping — **found them for a completely different reason than the one that produced the D'Arcy thirty-six.** There the gazetteer had not heard of the place and answered with something larger. Here FamilySearch's own collection file clusters a daughter village's dot beside its district town's. Same symptom, unrelated cause, and a test written against the symptom caught both. **A detector that only knows what a fault looks like travels between archives; one that knows why the fault happened does not.** The corollary is the reason to accept a neighbour's check even when confident: it is confidence that stops you running it, and the four pins had been published for weeks.

rows.lab: A field name that has to be checked against the code is a claim nobody can read
rows.text:
The research map stamped 1,065 of its 1,286 places `geo: "geonames-region"`. It reads as «pinned on the region's centroid» and means the exact opposite: **the place's own GeoNames coordinate, chosen from several same-named candidates by which one falls inside the expected bounding box.** The region does the choosing, never the placing — it is the thing that stopped Prato Carnico sitting on Prato in Tuscany.

**The session that wrote the label believed the label**, three weeks later, for about a minute, while auditing its own map for exactly that fault — and only stopped because it read the code. A neighbouring archive, told the story, said the obvious thing back: rename it, because a name that has to be verified against the source is not readable, and this archive's whole method is that a claim should be checkable by reading it.

It is now **`geonames-disambiguated`**, with the full table of provenance stamps and this reason written beside it in the generator, and the old value migrated on read so nothing carried forward out of the shipped file quietly keeps the old name. **The data never changed. Only the sentence it was telling did.**

rows.lab: Search your own archive before you search the film
rows.text:
An afternoon went on reading nineteen frames of a baptism register to find out who Vittorio Defranceschi's father was. The answer was in `burials.json`, in this repository, published on this site: *Vitorio Defranceschi … aged 54 … **kin: Antonio***. One grep would have had it.

**The failure has a shape worth naming.** The archive had ingested the burial index as *dates and places* — it drew them on a map and counted them — and never read the `kin` column as *relationships*. A field that is carried but not interpreted is invisible in exactly the way a missing field is, and it is worse, because its presence in the file makes the archive feel complete.

**So: before opening a register to answer a question about a person, grep every data file in the project for that person's name and read every column of every row that comes back** — not the columns the page happens to render. The same sweep that found the father also found his four children, which nobody had drawn either, and turned two loose witness lines into three generations.

rows.lab: A sweep that fails its target can still finish a family
rows.text:
Sixteen frames were read to find one baptism — Vittorio, son of Antonio — and it is not there. The whole of 1750 to 1760 now stands searched with **no Defranceschi child of any Antonio in it**, which is a real result and a wide one: it moves the question from *where in this volume* to *was he baptised in this parish at all*.

**The same frames handed over a different household almost complete.** Giacomo de Franceschi and Pascasia turn up as parents in 1750, 1753, 1756 and 1759 — four children, three forenames, one of them lost to smeared ink. **None of that was being looked for.** A page-by-page read collects everything on the page, and the entries you were not hunting are worth logging as carefully as the one you were, because the alternative is reading the same sixteen frames again in a month for the next question.

**The discipline that makes the by-catch usable is recording what you did not resolve.** Three godmother lines here style a wife of Jacobus as *Veneranda* where four baptisms say *Pascasia*; a godfather of 1754 is *«Jacobus filius Jacobi»* and cannot be the baby of 1753. Both are written down as open, not smoothed into the tidy version — because the tidy version would have merged two generations of one forename, which is the commonest way a parish reconstruction goes wrong.

rows.lab: «Figlio di» is worth more than a hundred appearances of the same two names
rows.text:
For two days this archive read **Gasparo** and **Giacomo** de Franceschi as two households at Svetvinčenat, because both stand godparent through the 1750s and both have a wife named in the entries. Then one line of 1762 — *«Gasparo **figlio di** M.o Giacomo de Franceschi»* — collapsed them into a father and his grown son, and a second instance four months later confirmed it.

**The lesson is about what godparent entries can and cannot carry.** Dozens of them establish that two forenames are active in a parish at once. **Not one of them establishes a relationship**, and the natural reading of two names appearing in parallel — two households — is the wrong one about as often as it is right. A single *«figlio di»*, *«q.»* or *«uxor»* outweighs the whole pile.

**So: when a sweep is producing the same two or three forenames over and over, stop counting appearances and start hunting for the one entry that says how they are related.** It will be rarer than the appearances and it will be worth more than all of them — here it also dated the son, because the volume's own index had his baptism twenty-five years earlier and the ages agreed.

rows.lab: An ingested index has columns nobody read
rows.text:
`fsrecords.json` has been in this repository for weeks. It was ingested for **names, dates and places**, which is what the pages built from it show. It also has a **parents** column, and until today nobody had looked at it.

In that column: *Franca De Franceschi, 8 Dec 1769, **parents Ano De Franceschi & Mattia***; *Pasqua Vitoria, 16 Dec 1773, **parents Giacomo De Franceschi & Nicoletta***; *Maria Matthia, 3 Sep 1784, **parents Victorii De Franceschi & Euphemię***. **Three generations, two of the archive's open questions answered, and a bridge from the marriage register to the baptism index** — all of it sitting in a file the site already reads from.
