**This is the second time in one day.** The morning's version was `burials.json`, ingested for dates and places, carrying a `kin` column that named Vittorio's father. **The pattern is not «we missed a file». It is «we ingested a source for the fields we wanted and never audited the fields we got».** The remedy is cheap and should be routine: for every ingested dataset, print the full key set and the distinct values of every column before deciding what the file is for.

rows.lab: Reading
rows.text:
**A hyphenated surname at a line break is the most dangerous place on the page.** Of five false readings killed by magnification in one sweep of the Svetvinčenat baptisms, **four sat in the godparent or parent slot and three broke the surname across a line** — *«An-/tonij Bergamo»* read as *Defranczo*, *«Domi-/nici»* read hopefully. The eye finishes the word from expectation, and the expectation is the surname you are hunting. **The rule: never write down a name that begins on one line and ends on the next until you have magnified it.**

**And the trap is not always the surname.** One of the five was *«Joanna filia q.m **Francisci** Zabrza»* — a **forename** that looks like the beginning of *Franceschi*.

rows.lab: Reading
rows.text: **A common forename identifies nobody.** *«Fosca uxor Dominici Defranceschi»* appears seven times in the Svetvinčenat baptisms and is a real, single woman. But the same volume also carries *«Fosca uxor Martini Merklem»* — a different Fosca, four entries away on the same leaf. **Before treating a forename as a person, check whether the parish used it once or used it constantly.** The full form is the evidence; the forename alone is a coincidence waiting to be published.

rows.lab: Reading
rows.text:
**A reading that would overturn an established fact is a warning, not a discovery.** Twice in one sweep of the Svetvinčenat baptisms a spread-scale glance produced something startling — a second wife for a man whose wife was already documented, and a baptism of the surname where none should be. **Both were false, and both died at magnification.** The ordinary readings held; the exciting ones did not.

**Excitement is a signal to slow down.** A finding that would rewrite the tree deserves *more* scrutiny than one that merely adds to it, not less — and the temptation runs precisely the other way.

rows.lab: Coverage
rows.text: **A negative from a volume read frame by frame is evidence. A negative from a volume searched by index is nothing.** The Svetvinčenat baptism register 1764–1791 has now been read at every one of its 127 openings. That is what lets this archive say, and mean, that **no child of Vittorio and Euphemia was baptised in it** — even though an index entry names one in 1784. **The index and the volume disagree, and only a complete read makes that disagreement visible** rather than invisible.

rows.lab: Coverage
rows.text:
**An index and a complete read are not rivals; each catches what the other drops.** This archive read all 127 openings of the Svetvinčenat baptism register 1764–1791 and **missed the 1784 baptism of Vittorio's daughter** — which the FamilySearch index had, and whose image ark pointed straight back at a frame already read and passed over.

**The reverse is equally true**: the index gives no godparents, no honorifics, no *«ex hac Parochia»*, and none of the sixty-odd godparent appearances that show where this family actually stood. **Run both, and check each against the other.** An index entry with an image ark is a free audit of your own reading — resolve it and go back to the frame.

rows.lab: Sources
rows.text:
**An ingested index's «birth» column may hold ages worked backwards from a burial, not baptisms.** `fsrecords.json` lists *«Vitorio Defranceschi, **1758**, parent Antonio»*, which reads exactly like a baptism record and was very nearly chased as one. The underlying entry is his **burial** — 8 November 1812, *aged 54* — and 1758 is FamilySearch's arithmetic, flagged on their own page as **«Birth Year (Estimated)»** and flattened to a bare number on ingest.

**A second one checked the same day behaves identically**: *«Mathęius De Franceschi, **1750**, parent Anton»* is a burial of 7 August 1819, *aged 69*. Both sit in the `6B47-` id range, and on this evidence that range is burials. *(Two records verified, not the whole range — stated as what was checked.)*

**An estimate that loses its label becomes a fact.** Check the event type on the record page before treating any ingested year as an act.

rows.lab: Sources
rows.text:
**Full-text search reads Italian civil registration, not the Croatia Church Books — so it reaches this family only during the Italian period.** Measured on 21 September 2026 by sampling the collection line of 97 of the 3,967 documents it returns for *Defranceschi*: Emilia-Romagna 70, Friuli and Lombardy 12, Sardinia, Veneto and Marche 11, the rest scattered, and **zero** from Croatia, Istria or Rijeka.

**That is why Rotilio's marriage was findable and Fiume's 1740s households are not.** His banns were posted at **Trieste in 1928**, in an Italian civil register. The Fiume baptisms of the 1740s are a Croatian church book. **Before querying, ask which archive the record would physically sit in** — the service's reach is geographic and administrative, not linguistic.

rows.lab: Reading
rows.text: **Quote the phrase, or full-text ORs your words and buries you.** *Defranceschi Valentino Fiume* returns **1,079,220** documents and the top hits are **Fiume Veneto, in Friuli** — a different town in a different country, matched on one word. The same query as `"Valentino Defranceschi"` returns **4**. **A result count in the millions is not a rich seam; it is a broken query.**

rows.lab: Coverage
rows.text:
**Renaming a person leaves their old page standing, because the dossier builder only ever adds.** *Maria Trompich (Cincopan)* was renamed to *Maria Trompich or Fumpich (Cincopan)* when the two copies of her daughter's marriage act turned out to disagree. The new page appeared; **the old one kept answering 200** on the live site, with the superseded single spelling on it. `build-dossiers.py` writes a dossier for every current person and **prunes nothing**, so the stale entry survived every rebuild until it was deleted by hand.

**After renaming or removing anyone, check that their old slug stopped resolving.** A page nobody links to is still a page a search engine can hand someone, and this one contradicted its replacement.

rows.lab: Reading
rows.text:
**Two goes at counting the orphans, two confident wrong answers — and the second was wronger than it looked.** Hunting for other stale pages, a first pass compared dossier slugs against roster names with a hand-written slugger and reported **229 orphans**. The slugger disagreed with the project's own on accented names — it turned *Mathæus* into `math-us-defranceschi` — so most of the 229 were real people the test simply could not match.

**Rerunning with `build-dossiers.py`'s own `slugify` gave 206, and that was still wrong**, because dossiers are not built from the roster alone. The list included in-laws drawn from other files — *Maria Valhart*, *Ruža Hreljac*, *Ana Kalanj* — and entries that are not people at all: *what-it-is*, *why-this-is-published*, *a-hundred-thousand-ducats*.

**The true count was one**, and it was the one already known about. **Borrowing the project's own function fixed the spelling of the question and not its logic** — and a number that survives one correction feels far more trustworthy than a number that has never been corrected at all. **Never mass-delete on a figure your own tooling produced without checking what the outliers actually are.**

rows.lab: Sources
rows.text:
**Every image in the Croatia collection carries a household index, and nobody here had opened one.** `/ark:/61903/3:1:<ark>?view=fullText` returns a transcript panel listing **every household on that plate** with its date and both parents — nineteen on one Fiume leaf. **That is an index at image level**, and it turns «which of these 200 frames is worth magnifying?» from a day of cropping into a page of reading.

**It does not replace the plate.** The first thing it produced was a surname this archive disputes — it reads a 1748 Fiume household as *Mancoschi* where this archive has *Defranceschi*. **Use it to choose frames, not to settle names.**

rows.lab: Reading
rows.text:
**Stop guessing crops as fractions; measure the plate.** Four attempts to isolate one Fiume entry failed because the crop window was being estimated by eye from a shrunken screenshot — and the estimate was badly wrong, putting the book in the plate's top-left quadrant when it actually fills **x 0.034–0.964, y 0.044–0.951**.

**The reliable method is local.** Fetch the plate once (`sg30p0` refuses a bare request, but the browser's redirect yields a signed S3 URL that serves it without a session), then find the page edges from column and row means, the gutter from the darkest interior column, and **the text lines from row STANDARD DEVIATION at full resolution**.

**Brightness thresholding finds nothing on these films** — the ink is too fine, and any downscale averages it into the paper; a 1/4-scale pass returned *zero* text lines on a page carrying dozens. **Variance found 35 lines on one page and 38 on the other.** That converts «somewhere on this plate» into «the fourth entry, lines 10 to 12».

rows.lab: Sources
rows.text:
**In the Croatia collection, a bare year in an ingested «birth» column is usually a burial's arithmetic.** Four records were caught this way in one day — *Vitorio 1758*, *Mathęius 1750*, *Mattio 1742*, *Antonio 1753* — and **every one is a burial**, whose record page says *Birth Year (Estimated)* and whose year is the clerk's stated age subtracted from the date of death.

**Ingest flattens that label away and leaves a number that reads exactly like a baptism.** Treat any bare year in this collection as an estimate until the record page has been opened. Reading them as births does not merely misdate people — **it invents them**, because the same person then appears once as a birth and once as a death.

rows.lab: Reading
rows.text:
**A surname search will hand you families whose only connection to the name is a mother.** Hunting Fiume marriages, two results read *«Maddalena Franceschi, spouse Gio Batta Franceschi»* — apparently the very couple being looked for. They are the marriages of **Giovanni Masatto in 1846 and Pietro Masatto in 1852**, a century later and a different family: *Franceschi* is the **mother's maiden name**, which the index has attached to the household as though it were the family's own surname.

**The tell was the date, and it was visible in the result list.** Check the century before the name — a surname index does not distinguish the family that bears a name from the family that married one.

rows.lab: A three-month hole in a marriage register is usually Lent
rows.text:
**Marriage registers go quiet every spring, and it is not damage.** Canon law closed the *tempus clausum* from **Ash Wednesday to Low Sunday**, so a Catholic parish records no weddings for six or seven weeks each year — and with the weeks either side thin, the silence can run to three months.

**This matters at a join.** Frames **191 and 192** of the Fiume film hand over from one sweep to another, and the dates jump from **25 February 1748** to **2 June 1748**. A missing leaf at exactly that point would be invisible and would quietly falsify a nil.

**Two checks settle it in a minute.** Read the **pencil foliation** on the outer corner of the right-hand page — at Fiume it runs one number per frame, and **181 → 182** across the gap says no leaf is missing. Then **compute Easter**: Ash Wednesday 1748 was **28 February**, three days after the last wedding.

**Do both wherever one session's reading meets another's.** *A gap you did not explain is a gap you cannot count as read.*

rows.lab: Check the comparison operator before you trust a catalogue's nil
rows.text:
**The Austrian State Archives' field search defaults to «starts with».** Type *Franceschi*, press Search, and you get **43 records with no Defranceschi in them** — a clean-looking, complete-looking, wrong answer. Change the operator to **«contains»** and the same term returns **99**.

**Every archive search box has a default, and almost none of them announces it.** Before recording a nil, run the query twice: once as given, once with the broadest operator the form offers. If the counts differ, the default was doing the searching.

**The general rule for this surname** is to search the **stem** — *Franceschi* — with *contains*. One pass then catches *De Franceschi*, *Defranceschi*, *de' Franceschi* and the adjacent diminutives together, and the diminutives can be discarded afterwards by eye. Separate queries per spelling cost round-trips and still miss the one you did not think of.

rows.lab: An index can name the right country and the wrong province
rows.text:
**The dangerous geocoding error is not the one that lands in another country.** That one is obvious and a country test catches it. The dangerous one keeps the country and moves the province: **«Fasana»** resolved to *Pont Canavese, Torino, Piemonte* instead of **Fažana in Istria** — five hundred kilometres, and *«Italia»* is true of both, because Fažana was Italian from 1918 to 1947.

**It survived because every check was pointed at the country.** The atlas had the dot right; the printed pages had it wrong; eight people were shown as born in the Alps.

**The test that finds it is a list of the provinces on the wrong side of the peninsula** — Piemonte, Lombardia, Toscana, Lazio, Campania, Sicilia and the rest — applied to any record whose parish this archive has already placed on the eastern Adriatic. It is in `place-audit.py`.

**And the fix keeps both strings.** The index's words stay on the record as provenance; the resolution is what prints. *Overwriting the source would hide the very error that had to be found.*

rows.lab: A godparent's husband is not evidence of which household she belongs to
rows.text:
**A baptism entry names its parents carefully and its godparents casually**, and the difference matters when a surname is common in one village.

**At Svetvinčenat in ten months of 1737–1739 the register gives *«uxor Jacobi de Franceschi»* three different wives** — **Anzola** in December 1737, **Agata** in August 1738, **Jacoba** in September 1738 — and then **Angela**, who is Anzola, in March 1739. *Angela is alive on both sides of the other two, so one man cannot have had all three.*

**And one of the three belongs to somebody else.** *Jacoba* is named six weeks earlier as the lawful wife of **Pietro** de Franceschi, in an entry where she is a **parent** and the clerk had every reason to be exact. **When the same woman turns up as a godmother he writes *«Jacoba uxor Jacobi»*** — a forename pulled, most likely, by her own.

**The working rule.** *Parents* in a baptism are evidence; *«wife of X»* in a godparent line is a label, and a weak one. **Use it to show that a household existed, never to decide which household a person was in** — and where a village has two men of one forename and surname, expect the register itself not to be able to tell them apart.

*Neither reading is preferred here. Both are recorded, because the alternative — picking one — would put a person in the wrong family and leave no trace of the choice.*

rows.lab: Read both exposures — a duplicate frame is not a redundant one
rows.text:
**Films repeat an opening more often than a reader expects**, and the repeat is usually treated as waste. At Svetvinčenat **images 120 and 121 are the same book page**, and they are not interchangeable: **loose slips are lying on the leaf, and they have shifted between the two shots**. What one frame hides the other shows.

**The slips themselves are records.** At this parish they are the priest's own memoranda — baptisms written out in **Italian** on scraps and kept inside the Latin register, photographed where they lay. *A sweep that skips them loses entries that are in no index and on no page.*

**So: before writing down that an opening does not contain something, check whether the film shot it twice** — the page numbers in the outer corner settle it in seconds — **and read the slips as well as the leaf.**

rows.lab: Never date a frame from its year heading alone
rows.text:
**A page headed *1759* whose entries are all dated *1739* is not a contradiction; it is one clerk's 3.** On images 123 and 126 of the Svetvinčenat births the heading reads five and the entries beneath it read three, and the page numbers run straight on from the frame before.

**Three cheap cross-checks, in order of reliability.** The **page number** in the outer corner, which cannot lie about sequence; the **entry dates** inside the page, which the clerk wrote more carefully than the heading; and only then the **heading**.

*This nearly put a household twenty years out of place.* A baptism read as 1759 and published as such would have been attached to the wrong generation, and nothing downstream would ever have questioned it.

rows.lab: Point a check at the build you just made, by name
rows.text:
**A gate that reads `dist` in a shared working tree is not reading your work.** Several sessions build out of one checkout here, so `dist` routinely holds a half-written build or another session's data — and a check pointed at it passes or fails on somebody else's page.

**This archive's gate builds into `dist-gate-$$` and passes `--dist` to every check explicitly**, which is why a kit bug reported on 22 September — four tools ignoring the `ARCHIVE_OUT` variable because a command-line flag overrode it — **could not reach it**. The flag was already pointing at the right place.

**Verified rather than assumed, the same day.** A fresh 1,475-page build was made by hand and the living check run against it by name: *«no living person reaches the build — 52 living, 0 dates guarded»*. **That is the sentence the living rule needs, and it is worth nothing unless the directory in it is the one you just built.**

rows.lab: Test a correction against the page it names, not against the site
rows.text:
**A self-correcting archive quotes the wording it is retiring**, so searching the whole site for a corrected phrase returns mostly the corrections themselves. Run that way on 22 September it flagged **41** claims; every one sampled was the old wording being quoted properly.

**Narrowing it to the data files that build the page each correction names** cuts it to **21**, and excluding any occurrence sitting within five hundred characters of *corrected, withdrawn, retired, no longer, used to* cuts it to **12**. **Ten of the twelve are transcriptions** — a register's own words, which are supposed to survive.

**The two that were real were both about pointing rather than asserting**: a search-register row that still gave a superseded count with no link to the correction, and an entry of 1728 that nobody had connected to a question raised four days later. *The value of the check was not in what it found wrong; it was in what it made somebody read again.*

rows.lab: Never stage a directory in a tree other sessions build in
rows.text:
**`git add <directory>` publishes whatever is sitting in that directory, including work you have never seen.** In this checkout several Claude sessions build at once, and on 22 September 2026 two commits made here carried other sessions' unstaged files — a kit pin bump, and 51 lines of the estate stylesheet. Both were correct changes. Neither was a choice.

**Stage files by name, and check before committing.** `scripts/whose.sh` prints the staged set in two halves — **this archive's** (`site/src/data`, `site/src/pages`, `scripts`, `data`) and **shared ground** (`site/public`, layouts, components, the kit pin, the repository root) — and **fails if shared ground is staged** without `--allow-shared`.

**The general form is worth more than the rule.** *A guard that only warns is a guard you learn to scroll past; the one that stops you is the one that works.* This archive had already written the lesson as prose four commits before it repeated the mistake.

rows.lab: When an origin keeps turning up, stop reading it as one man's biography
rows.text:
**«ex Cargn.» / «ex Cargnia» / «ex Cargno» — Carnia, the mountain corner of Friuli — is the only origin the Svetvinčenat register ever gives anyone of this surname.** For a day this archive read that as a fact about one man: *Joannes Baptista de Franceschi, an incomer.*

**Reading forward four more frames turned it into a fact about the parish.** Between 1742 and 1745 the same clerk writes *«ex Cargno»* against **seventeen different people**: Joannes Baptista Defranceschi (1742, 1743, **1744**), **Antonij Fiorca ex Cargno** standing godfather to a foundling on 9 April 1744, **Antonius Valentinus Colovri ex Cargno** standing godfather to Pietro Defranceschi's son on 14 February 1745 — *and the child is named Valentinus after him* — **Antonio Fabris ex Cargno** on 7 April 1746, **Jacobus Calavaris ex Cargna** on 22 January 1744, and **Antonius Fiasolo ex Cargno** in February 1744.

**A surname plus an origin is a biography. An origin that recurs across unrelated surnames is a migration.** Carnic men were at the castle in numbers in the 1740s, they stood at each other's fonts, and the Defranceschi were among them rather than exceptional to them.

**What it changes for the search.** The question stops being *«which Carnic parish did this man come from»* and becomes *«which Carnic parishes fed Svetvinčenat in the 1730s and 1740s»* — a question the Antenati registers for the Carnia comuni can be asked directly, and one where the other surnames (**Fiorca**, **Colovri**) are as good a handle as the name this archive is named for. *Recorded 23 September 2026.*

**27 September 2026 — reading to the end of the stretch takes it to roughly seventeen people across eleven surnames, 1742 to 1753.** Beside the Defranceschi: **Fiorasso** (Benedictus, Antonius, Joannes), **Merlin** (Mathias, Nicolaus), **Micaij** (Joannes Baptista, Nicolai), **Serban**, **Kiacovis**, **Cavang**, **Fiorid**, **Calavaris**, **Fiorca/Fiasolo**, **Colovri**, **Fabris**, **Bicicardi**. *They stand at each other's fonts and at the Defranceschi fonts.* **A colony, and the research question is now which Carnic parishes fed this castle rather than which one a single man came from.**

rows.lab: A directory can be silent and still be somebody's desk
rows.text:
**On 27 September this archive moved the whole estate out of iCloud Drive, and waited for the machine to go quiet before doing it.** The wait was for `astro`, `node` and `npm` to fall silent across all fifteen directories, for forty-five continuous seconds. It looked careful. It was not enough, twice over.

**It never watched `git`.** Repacks fire from `gc.auto` on git's own schedule, triggered by ordinary commits rather than by anything a session is visibly doing — so there is no process to wait for. Three archives were left holding interrupted `tmp_pack` files, and one lost **95 objects**, all of them binaries: scans and document images. *They were recoverable only because they were pushed.*

**And a poll cannot see an editor.** The Falco session, about to swap in a verified fresh clone, found that archive's `package.json` and `package-lock.json` had been written **forty-five seconds earlier** — a kit repin and a whole new gate, uncommitted, existing nowhere else. A swap would have destroyed it silently. Nothing was running; somebody was simply typing.

**The signal is not quiet. It is `git status --porcelain` plus the mtimes on the manifest, taken twice a minute apart.** A directory with no processes in it can still be someone's desk.

**Two more things learned by doing this one badly.** *`git gc` does not clear those stale `tmp_pack` files* — git only prunes temporaries older than a day, so an archive that runs housekeeping still carries them and must remove them by name. And **a fresh clone cannot be verified inside the estate**: `checkpages` counts every directory as an archive, and because its rule is «a page in three or more archives is shared», one phantom duplicate can reclassify pages as shared *for every archive at once*, not merely for the one that made it.

*The move itself was right — an iCloud-synced git directory had already reverted refs, emptied five object stores, removed 96 tracked files and rolled 35 more back to older, smaller, still-valid versions. The damage was done before anything was moved. But a careful-looking wait that watches the loud processes and not the one holding the lock is the same fault as every other one found this week: **the check that was easy to write rather than the one that would have failed.***

rows.lab: A formula that lies can be convicted, but only where the truth is known another way
rows.text:
**This archive has said since September that the Svetvinčenat godparent formula is unreliable about husbands' forenames.** It was inferred in 1738 from *«Agata uxor Jacobi»* and *«Jacoba uxor Jacobi»* appearing inside the years Anzola was alive — *three wives in ten months, at least one of them wrong.* **But which one was wrong could not be said**, because there was nothing independent to check any of them against. The doubt was the whole finding.

**On 27 September the same register convicted itself.** *«**Pascasia uxor Caspari Defranceschi**»* stands on **16 December 1751** and again on **3 February 1752**. And on **29 April 1753** the register writes *«patrini fuerunt, **Jacobus Defranceschi, et Pascasia ejus uxor**»* — **husband and wife in one phrase, in one hand.** Pascasia also bears Jacobo three children in full parental entries, 1746, 1747 and 1750. *Caspar's wife, six times over between 1744 and 1749, is **Maria**.*

**So the two entries are not doubtful. They are wrong, and they are demonstrably wrong, and the same clerk made the same mistake about the same woman fourteen months apart.**

**The method point is the shape, not the instance.** *A source that errs can only be shown to err where the truth is recoverable from somewhere else — a parental entry, a joint line, a second series.* **Where it is not, the honest output is a doubt and not a ruling**, which is what 1738 got and should keep. **An archive that convicts a source on internal inconsistency alone is guessing which half to believe.**

rows.lab: To ask whether a nil is real, ask the index about the place and not about a name
rows.text:
**A search that returns nothing has two meanings and they are not close together**: *nobody of that name lived there*, or *the index does not cover the place*. **Publishing the first when the truth is the second puts a negative in the archive that is about the catalogue and reads as though it were about the family.**

**The instinct is to test with a common surname, and it is a bad instinct.** *On 27 September this archive tested eleven Carnia comuni with «Rossi» — which returns nothing anywhere in Carnia, because Rossi is a name of the plains.* **A control that is absent for real reasons cannot distinguish absence from silence.** Carnic surnames — *Della Pietra*, *Puntel*, *Craighero* — did better and still left eleven comuni unanswered, because no three surnames cover a valley.

**The answer is to stop asking about names.** *Query the index for the PLACE alone — `?localita=X` with no surname — and it answers the only question that matters: does this catalogue hold this comune?* **Eighteen comuni, one pass, no guessing: fifteen indexed, three absent.** *Thirteen nils became real negatives and three stayed honestly unknown.*

*The general form: **when a nil result is the finding, test the instrument and not the subject.***

rows.lab: Two rows with the same ark are not similar people, they are one record entered twice
rows.text:
**Duplicate detection in a one-name study is usually a matter of judgement**: *the same name, the same year, the same parish — and no way to tell a repeated entry from a cousin named after the same grandfather.* **This archive spent weeks treating it that way, and folded names four different ways looking for a better guess.**

**It was the wrong question.** *A row that came from a FamilySearch index carries the `ark` of the record it came from. Two rows carrying the SAME ark did not come from two records about two people — they came from ONE record, read twice, by two different passes that spelled the name differently.* **That is documentary proof of a duplicate and it needs no judgement at all.**

*Of thirty-six suspicious groups, eighteen pairs were settled this way in a single comparison. **And the same field settles the opposite case**: seven pairs carry two DIFFERENT arks, which proves they rest on two records and must not be merged on a resemblance.*

**The trap that nearly cost three men their pages:** *grouping by name alone swept «Giovanni De Franceschi 1829» into a single verdict, when the group held a proven ark-duplicate AND a separate Fiume shoemaker.* **Adjudicate PAIRS, not groups** — *a group of three can be one duplicate and one distinct person at the same time, and a verdict on the group is wrong for half of it.*

*The general form: **before judging whether two records describe one person, check whether they are the same record.***

rows.lab: A check that counts can be satisfied without being answered
rows.text:
**`check:sources` counts hosts this archive links to and never describes. It cannot tell a description from a sentence of the right shape.** *Seventy-three hosts stood undescribed, and forty-six of them already had full entries on the research register — so the fastest honest-looking fix was a generator: «this archive has gone to it N times; what it gave is on the register».* **That passes. It also produces precisely the thing the check exists to prevent** — *a citation with no account of itself, now with a paragraph attached.*

**The second temptation was worse, because it was accurate.** *Five of the seventy-three are not sources at all: an image-delivery host, a permalink host, and three URLs that appear only inside the **credit** field of a Wikimedia Commons record — the attribution chain a public-domain licence carries with it.* **Writing «Yale University Art Gallery» its own bibliography line would have cleared the count and told the reader something false about where this archive has been.** *They belong on the entry of the source that carries them, and that is where they went.*

*The general form: **when a check counts, ask what it would count as success, and then ask whether that is the thing you wanted.** A gate is a floor and never a specification.*

rows.lab: A shared component answers its own question, not necessarily yours
rows.text:
**The notables table asked «is this person linked to this family?» and rendered the answer through a component that grades «how well is this claim evidenced?».** *Those are different questions and the mismatch was invisible, because the component has a default.*

**Its five levels are documented, probable, inferred, family and disputed, and its alias table folds anything it does not recognise — `no` and `open` included — down to «family».** *So `conn: "no"` came out as a badge reading **«Family»**, in a column headed **«Link to this family»**, against six people this archive states are not related — **Piero della Francesca among them**.* **Two lines above, the page's own dek says a shared patronymic is not a shared ancestor and that saying otherwise is how family myths start.** *The table had been saying otherwise, in one word, ever since the component was adopted.*

**Nothing was broken and nothing failed.** *The component is correct for its own question; the gate has no way to know that a five-level grade was being asked a yes-or-no one; and a fallback that always returns a valid-looking answer cannot report that it was never given a valid input.*

*The general form: **when you pass your data to something shared, check what it does with the values it does not recognise.** A default is the place where a category error goes quiet.*

rows.lab: One field name, three meanings — which is why no total function could be written
rows.text:
**The landing-site session's answer to the «Family» badge was to make an unknown level render «Ungraded»; D'Arcy's was better — they made their grading function TOTAL, so no unknown exists to render.** *A total function does beat a loud default **where the set is closed**. Here it is not, and the reason is the finding.*

**This archive uses `conf` in four data files and it means three different things.** *In `families.json` and `explorer.json` it grades a claim — doc, inf, lore, probable, strong. In `gists.json` it also takes **`neg`**, which is not a grade at all but the archive stating a thing is **NOT** so: «Carlo's own published history never makes the Carnia claim». In `ancestors.json` it also takes **`living`**, which is a person's status.* **A grade, a negation and a person marker, under one key.**

*No honest total function can be written over that domain, because the domain is not one domain. **Until the field is split, a loud default is the correct answer and «Ungraded» is the right thing for it to say.***

**Three fallbacks of this archive's own were pointing the wrong way.** *The notables column resolved unknown to «Family» and was publishing it — six unrelated people, Piero della Francesca among them. The destinations ternary resolved anything-not-doc-or-inf to «lore», so a **`neg`** would have been badged «Family»: not a mis-grade but the opposite of the finding. The Giornaletto map knew only doc and inf and fell back to **«Inferred»**. And the tree's fallback — unreachable, because its three values are all covered — pointed at **«Documented»**, the strongest grade in the set.*

**The rule, which the kit had already written in one file and broken in another:** *AncChart resolves an unknown confidence to neutral grey; Evidence resolved one to «Family». **Grey asserts nothing. «Family» asserts kinship.*** *Where a fallback cannot be avoided it must land on something that makes no claim — and the direction of a default matters more than its existence, because a default is never exercised by the cases anyone thought about.*

rows.lab: A line beginning «ok» does not get read
rows.text:
**The landing-site session found D'Arcy running on a kit pin nobody had noticed had changed — and the build had printed the correct pin three times that day.** *The instrument was not silent. It was unread.*

**This gate prints thirteen «ok» lines and, under them, nine steady numbers**: *55 living, 595 people across the evidence files, 425 attested name cells, 136 of 155 sources reachable.* **Every one is restated identically each build, so every one is invisible.** *If a living person's flag were dropped the count would fall from 55 to 54 and the gate would still say «ok» — a silent regression in the one number in this archive that must never be wrong.*

**So the numbers are written to `data/gate-witness.json` and COMMITTED, and the check speaks only when one MOVES.** *Committing does two things printing cannot: a number that shifts inside an unrelated commit shows up as a diff in a file whose only subject is these numbers, and the file's history becomes the history of the archive's shape.* **It does not fail on movement** — *nearly every number moves for good reasons, and a gate that cried at every change would be switched off within a day.* It fails only when it cannot read the archive, *because a witness reporting «no change» after failing to look is the fault it exists to catch.*

**And wiring it in reproduced that fault one level up.** *The gate's `run()` helper prints a check's output only when the check FAILS.* **Passed through it, the witness was silent in precisely the case it was written for**: *a test movement of 99 → 59 printed «ok witness» and not one word more.* **The harness was hiding the only line meant to be read.** *The witness is now run outside the wrapper.*

*Two independent counts agreeing is worth the duplication: this file measures 59 living rows under 55 names, reading the data itself, and the kit's own harvest — different code, different author — reports 55. **A number is only confirmed when something that did not compute it agrees.***

rows.lab: A count cannot see a substitution
rows.text:
**Between a pin and a witness there is a third kind of value, and the D'Arcy session found it: a DECISION.** *A pin has one correct value, so speaking on any move is right. A count has no correct value, only a history, so failing on movement would be a gate switched off inside a day. A decision is neither — it is a judgement made once, and changing it should require a deliberate act.*

**The one this archive needed is the one no number could have given.** *Person ids are minted once and never derived, because a derived id moves when a birth year is corrected and a moved id is a dead URL.* **`check-witness.py` counts them — 1,446 — and that count is exactly the same whether or not one of them now points at a different human being.** *Delete a person, mint a new one, and the number does not flinch. **A count cannot see a substitution**, and no other figure in this archive can either.*

*So the pid mapping is **declared** rather than counted: 1,446 ids against the person each one addresses. **Adding is free.** Changing or removing refuses, and the diff names the person whose address moved.* **Two scalars are declared beside it** — *the kit pin, because D'Arcy ran a day on a pin carried by a commit about something else; and the living policy `named-bare`, because every other check reads that flag rather than deciding it, so weakening it would quietly widen what may publish while all thirteen gates still said «ok».*

**All five refusals were provoked on purpose before the thing was wired in** — *pin moved, policy weakened, a pid reused for another person, a published pid vanished, a new pid added.* *The fifth must pass, and did.* **Watching a check refuse is the only evidence it can**: *a gate that has never been shown a bad input is a gate with no demonstrated behaviour, which is how «0 living» and «357 of 357» were both believed.*

rows.lab: A year copied because two rows share a name is not evidence
rows.text:
**Twenty-five rows in this archive were given their dates by name-matching against other rows in the same archive**, recorded honestly as `yfrom: «a dated entry already in this project's own burials data»` — *and then printed on person pages as though they were read off a register.*

**Five women called Maria Defranceschi all carried «1757–1757».** *Browachio, Buman, Contossich, Covaz, Dobrez — five different married surnames, one pair of dates, taken from a single Rijeka burial.* **That is impossible on its face and nobody looked**, because each row on its own page looked like an ordinary dated person. *Browachio's own record is her daughter's birth at **Termeno, Bolzano, in 1907**. Contossich's is her **marriage in 1788**. Julius, published as born in 1833, appears in **1829 as the father** at his daughter's baptism.*

**The tell was visible without opening a single record**: *identical dates across rows distinguished only by a married surname.* **A married surname is proof the woman lived to marry**, and every one of those five was published as having died in infancy.

*Two further things this cost. **A row may not belong to the family at all** — «Maria Defranceschi (Covaz)» rests on the baptism of Mariam **Covaz**, both parents Covaz, with the name Defranceschi nowhere in it. And **a row may sit on a record for a different person in a different country** — «Giacomo Defranceschi, d. 2012, Broken Hill» rests on the 1909 baptism of **Germano Defranceschi at Cloz, Trento**.*

*The general form: **a field recording where a value came from is not the same as a field recording that the value is true.** `yfrom` was honest about the borrowing and the page was not, and an archive that prints a provenance note beside a fabricated year has documented its own error without noticing it.*

rows.lab: Thirty-five of a hundred and seventy hits were one dead painter's name in a sale list
rows.text:
**Trove's pre-1940 results for this name are dominated by one heading — «Advertising» — thirty-five times, in the Argus, the Age, the Sydney Morning Herald and the Mercury, from 1879 to 1921.** *A count alone would read as a family trading in Melbourne for forty years.*

**They are auction catalogues.** *Every one lists **«M. DE FRANCESCHI»** among a column of painters — Cattermole, Kilburne, Ten Kate, Streeton, Chevalier — because a Roman painter's canvases were being sold at Gemmell, Tuckett & Co. **Mariano de Franceschi, born 1849, is already on this archive's own notables page**, and thirty-five of its Australian «hits» are his signature in a sale list.*

**This is the ANNO street-name lesson again and it did not announce itself**: *there the name was a Pola street and the hits were classified ads; here it is a painter and the hits are auction columns. In both, **the name is in the paper and the person is not in the country**.*

**What the remaining pre-1940 articles actually hold, once the painter is subtracted:** *a **Franceski household at Lismore** — a doctor, a Miss Franceski, **Amelia** the music teacher who became Mrs Sullivan, and **Caesar** of North Lismore showing persimmons and olives at the Sydney Royal Show; a **G. Franceski racing bicycles at Beverley, Western Australia**; **Annie Amanda Franceski Kean**, divorced at Maryborough in 1901 and carrying the name in the position a maiden surname survives in; and **Rev. Joseph de Franceschi, C.M.**, a Vincentian in Rio de Janeiro in 1912 and Regional Director for Brazil in 1930.* **Ten real people, under thirty-five advertisements for a dead man's paintings.**

*The general form: **a heading that repeats is a finding about the newspaper, not about the family**, and the only way to tell which is to read one.*

rows.lab: The terms a source was granted on may live in another archive entirely
rows.text:
**A Trove API key arrived on 27 September and this archive used it hard and well within the hour** — 170 articles harvested, a spelling trap found, a family put on a pin. *It also broke the written promise the key had been issued on, because that promise was in a different repository and nobody here had read it.*

**David answered four questions from the National Library on 20 September to get the key.** *One answer says: «**No full text of any article would be retrieved. The request is metadata only** — newspaper and gazette titles, their place coverage and their date ranges.»* **This archive searched article records, published 53 article snippets to a public remote, and fetched the text of about seventy articles from the Library's own website.**

*The D'Arcy session found it, said so to this archive and to David in the same breath, touched nothing, and was right on every point — **including the distinction that saves the work**: a heading, a date, a page and a URL are a **citation**; a snippet is **content**. The first is defensible and is the more useful half.*

**The general form, and it is not about Trove.** *A credential carries terms, and **the terms are not always where the credential is**. A key handed over in a chat window arrives with no conditions attached to it; the conditions were agreed somewhere else, by someone else, possibly for a different archive in the same estate.* **Before using a granted credential, find what was promised to get it** — *and if it cannot be found, ask, because «I was given a key» is not the same as «I was given permission».*

*The second lesson is smaller and sharper: **a repository is a publication**. The snippets were not shown on any page; they sat in a data file. They were public the moment they were pushed.*

rows.lab: A hundred of a hundred and twenty-eight, quoted as all of them
rows.text:
**The best instrument finding of the day nearly went into a letter to a national library on a measurement that did not support it.**

*Trove returns **13** newspaper articles for «Defranceschi» and **128** for «De Franceschi», and the striking part was that they **overlap by three** — the two spellings are nearly disjoint corpora, not one corpus the index folds together.* **The overlap was measured by pulling the 13 fused ids and the first 100 spaced ids and intersecting them.** *One hundred of one hundred and twenty-eight.* **The other twenty-eight were never compared, so the true overlap could have been anything from 3 to 13, and «they overlap by three» was a statement about the page size.**

*It survived: the complete harvest shows «De Franceschi» contributed **125 records not already held**, so exactly three were, and the id-level test places all three in the fused set. **Two derivations, one answer** — which is the only reason it is now safe to state.*

**The tell was available without any recheck**: *a default page of 100 against a total of 128.* *Whenever a comparison is made against «the results», ask how many results were actually in hand — **a paged API hands you a page and lets you call it the set**.*

*And the reason it got caught is worth more than the number: it was going into a document with someone else's name on it, sent to an institution that could withdraw a credential from seven archives. **A figure bound for somewhere consequential gets a second derivation; the same figure bound for a page here had already had one and passed.** The standard should not depend on the destination, and today it did.*

rows.lab: We do not test tools, we test tools while the last failure is still stinging
rows.text:
**The tool-you-do-not-run line is too comfortable, and the D'Arcy session found the sharper version of it.**

*Today this archive built a witness that speaks only when a number moves, wired it through a wrapper that swallows output on success, and it went silent in exactly the case it was written for — **four minutes** after the docstring explaining why unread output is the problem. Four hours later it built `check-decisions.py` and **provoked all five of its refusals on purpose before wiring it in**: pin moved, policy weakened, a pid reused, a published pid vanished, a new pid added. It caught two real faults inside the hour.*

**Same session, same day, same hands. The difference was not skill and it was not a rule. It was having been burned recently enough to bother.**

*D'Arcy then applied that to their own work and found the shape exactly: their decisions check had **four states tested and two untested, and the two untested were the two written last**. **They stopped testing at the point they stopped feeling burned**, and the boundary fell in the middle of one file.*

**So the honest statement is not «run your tools».** *It is that testing is powered by a recent failure, the charge runs down, and **the interval is short** — measured here in hours, and visible as a boundary inside a single file.* *Provoking every refusal before wiring a check in is the nearest thing to a fix, and it only works while somebody still remembers why it is the rule.*

*Which is the argument for [the method page](/method/) existing at all: **a lesson written down outlasts the sting that produced it**, and is the only part of it that does.*

rows.lab: grep matched the failure and && carried on
rows.text:
**A red gate was committed and pushed today, and the reason is four characters long.**

*The habit all day has been `./scripts/gate-isolated.sh | grep -E "ALL GREEN|FAIL|witness" && git commit`. **`grep` exits 0 when it finds a match**, and it found `FAIL`. So the failure printed on screen, `grep` reported success, `&&` did what it was told, and the commit went out on a gate that had just refused the change.*

**The gate was right and the finding was real**: *a man born in 1932 had been given a printed birth year; he would be 94, no death is recorded, and this archive gives a person who may be living a name and a town and nothing else.* *Fixed, and the date now sits in his note as what the document says rather than as what this archive asserts about him.*

**What makes this worth writing down is the shape, not the typo.** *The whole day's lesson has been that a check which cannot speak is no check — and here the check spoke, clearly, in the terminal, and the pipeline read its own output as approval.* **An instrument that reports and a gate that gates are different things, and piping one into a boolean turns the second into the first.**

*The fix is to test the SCRIPT's exit status and never a filter's: run the gate, capture `$?`, and let the filter only decide what gets printed. **A command that decides whether to proceed must be the command that did the work.***

rows.lab: The same ark proves one record; two arks do not prove two
rows.text:
**This morning's rule closed eighteen duplicate questions in a single comparison: two rows carrying the SAME FamilySearch ark came from one record read twice.** *It was stated as working in both directions — same ark, one record; different arks, two records — and the second half is false.*

**Mariam de Franceschi has two arks and one baptism.** *`1:1:QLYD-H7YJ` sits in «Croatia, Delnice Deanery Catholic Church Books, 1571–1926» and `1:1:QKMD-LKFC` in «Croatia, Church Books, 1516–1994», and both are **the baptism of 9 September 1632 at Rijeka**. **Two collections overlap on one parish**, so one event carries two identifiers.*

*The corrected rule: **an identifier proves identity, never difference.** A shared ark is proof of one record; separate arks are the absence of that proof and nothing more — which is why the seven «different arks» pairs had to be opened one at a time, and why doing so split them four to three rather than seven to nothing.*

**What settled all seven was not the ark at all. It was the parents.** *Two Elisabettas at Fiume in 1810 look identical until one has a father called Franco and the other parents called Anna and Andrea. Bortolo's burial and Bortolo's marriage look like two men until both name Gio Batta.* **In a parish where a dozen households share a surname, the discriminating field is the generation above**, and an index row that omits it cannot settle anything on its own.*

rows.lab: Having a name for a mistake is not protection against it
rows.text:
**On 27 September this archive closed an item whose subject was dates copied onto the wrong person, and catalogued the shapes the error takes.** *One of them was named **«the right person at the wrong century»** — Anna Maria really is a Defranceschi baptised at Fiume, in 1801 and not 1844; Pietro in 1803 and not 1884.*

**The closing paragraph of that same item then attached both of them to Valentino × Helena, whose children stop in 1757.** *Right family, right port, **wrong generation by two** — written inside a commit describing that exact error in other people's work.*

*What caught it was not vigilance but arithmetic done later: **Helena's children run 1737–1757 and a woman does not bear a child in 1801**, and Pietro's act names his mother as **Ursula**. The real household is Valentinus, born 1775/76, who married **Ursula de Berzoni** at Fiume on 6 October 1793.*

**The general form: a taxonomy of errors reads like a defence and is not one.** *Naming a failure mode makes it easier to describe afterwards, not harder to commit — the recognition happens in the write-up and the mistake happens in the reasoning, and they are different passes.* **The only thing that actually caught it was checking a date against a lifespan**, which is the cheapest test in genealogy and is not performed by knowing that it exists.

rows.lab: Record the film and the frame, never only the ark
rows.text:
**A long register sweep pinned its working state in four scratchpad files — hundreds of pre-resolved image arks for Svetvinčenat's baptism, index and marriage volumes.** *The scratchpad is session-local. It was cleared between sessions and every one of them is gone.*

**What survived is what had been written into the archive itself**: *the film number, the frame numbers, the date anchors, and which frames had already been read.* **From those the arks can be rebuilt in three calls; from the arks alone, nothing could have been rebuilt at all** — an ark is an opaque token that says neither which film it belongs to nor which frame.

*The rebuild also documented a route that is three hops and guessable at none of them: **`dgs%3A<FILM>_<FRAME>` → apid**, then **navigate** (never `fetch` — cross-origin returns 401) to `sg30p0…/<apid>/dist.jpg`, which redirects to a **signed S3 URL valid one hour** that `curl` will serve at full resolution, where `curl` against FamilySearch itself is refused outright.*

*The general form: **cache the derived, record the derivable.** A note that says «arks are in the scratchpad» is a note that expires silently; a note that says «film 005497885, frames 115–162, read 115–123 and 125–127» is one that can be resumed from in any session, by anyone, after any cache is lost.*

rows.lab: A hand is only legible against itself
rows.text:
**This archive read one word wrong for five days, published a conclusion on it, and could not see the error by looking harder at the word.**

*The mother of a child baptised in 1743 was read as «**Francisca**». She is «**Pascasia**». Magnifying the word from 2.4× to 8× did not settle it — at every scale it was a plausible squiggle, and the reader kept supplying the name already in mind, because a Francisca **was** in that parish and Pascasia was not yet known to be.*

**What settled it was refusing to read the word alone.** *The same clerk had written both candidate names elsewhere in the same volume: his «**Franciscus**» on the facing leaf, eight weeks later, and his «**Pascasia**» nine images on, in a baptism this archive had already transcribed correctly. Set at one magnification side by side, the disputed word is the second stroke for stroke and shares two letters with the first.*

**The rule that follows.** *Before a doubtful name is written down, find the same scribe writing **both** the name you think it is and the name you fear it is, elsewhere in the same book, and put all three at one magnification.* **A letterform has no meaning in isolation; it only means something against the same pen's other attempts at the same letter.**

*The same session made the inverse error and caught it the same way: two faint godmother lines were read as a repeat of the word freshly in mind, and at 7× with contrast they were the two different names already published. **Three false readings in one day, all from a pattern being carried from the frame before, all killed by a control.***

rows.lab: The archive was keeping its own triage list, in its prose
rows.text:
**Twenty-one published readings rested on one film. Re-reading them all at magnification is days of work, so which first?**

*The answer was already written down. **Seventeen of the notes say «magnified» or «read letter by letter». Four do not.*** *Those four were re-read first.*

**The one that had never claimed magnification carried two errors.** *The three that claimed it were checked as controls and all three held.*

**A small sample and not a guarantee** — *but a defensible order to work in, and far cheaper than twenty-one blind re-reads.* **An archive that records how carefully each claim was made can later sort its own claims by how much they deserve to be doubted.** *That is only true if the note is honest when the reading was quick, which is the harder half of the habit.*

rows.lab: Do not read social rank off an abbreviation
rows.text:
**A Gasparo de Franceschi is «M.ro» — Maestro, a master craftsman — in 1762, and «D.no» — Domino — twice in 1766.** *It is tempting to read a rise in the world.*

**The scribe changed in between.** *Arciprete Simon Zadro's loose Italian gives way to D. Mattio Adamich, who styles very nearly everyone «D.no».* **The abbreviation is a habit of the pen, not a promotion.**

*What actually identified the man was not a style of address but a **patronymic**: «Gaspare de Franceschi **q.m Ant.o** ex hoc Castro», which excluded two of three candidates outright because both were sons of a Jacobo, named as such in their own baptisms.* **One word of kinship outranks any amount of inference from titles.**

rows.lab: A spelling list is an instrument, and it belongs in the log with its counts
rows.text:
**This archive searched a newspaper portal, wrote «zero in every spelling», and was wrong twice over.**

*«Every spelling» meant **two**. The two not tried were the two that mattered: **`De Franceschi` spaced**, which reaches a whole journal the unspaced form does not, and **`Defrančeski`** in Croatian orthography, which is how a Croatian paper actually prints the name.* **One of them found the moment Carlo de Franceschi was told to become a historian. The other found a man at Ližnjan nobody knew existed.**

**And one spelling had to be thrown away.** *`Franceski` returns **1332** results because Croatian OCR renders **«francuski» — «French»** close enough to match.* **A count that large is a language, not a family**, and a sweep that banked it would have drowned in adjectives.

**The rule:** *record the terms and their counts, every time, in the search log — never in prose as «every spelling».* **A nil you cannot audit is not a finding, it is a stopping place**, and it tells the next reader to stop too.

rows.lab: When the priest changes, the surname changes — and the index loses you
rows.text:
**On 29 April 1782 this family stops being «Defranceschi» and starts being «Franceschi», and nothing happened to the family.**

*The parish of Svetvinčenat changed archpriest. **D. Antonio Massalini** had written the name as one word for twenty years; **D. Paolo Cossaich** writes it as two, without the «De». Six weeks later he writes «**Capo** Antonio de Franceschi» — «de» restored, spaced.* **Three spellings of one household inside three months, and the household did not move, marry out or change anything about itself.**

**⚠ This is where a name-indexed search silently fails.** *A reader searching an index for «Defranceschi» in the Svetvinčenat marriages finds the family up to 1782 and then loses it — not because the entries stop but because the clerk's hand changed.* **The gap would look exactly like a family leaving the parish.**

**So: a surname is a property of the scribe, not only of the person.** *Before concluding a family left a place, establish who was writing the book on the date the trail stops — and read forward past it in the images rather than the index.* **This archive found it only because it was reading the film frame by frame.**

*(The same lesson from the other end: [a spelling list is an instrument](/method/), and the two spellings not tried are always the two that matter.)*

rows.lab: A parish register records where the couple were, not where the parish is
rows.text:
**On 13 March 1783 a Svetvinčenat couple were married at Parenzo, and the act is in the Svetvinčenat book.**

*«…furono interrogati da me sottoscritto **nella Chiesa della B.V. degli Angioli di Parenzo**» — Vittorio de Franceschi and Eufemia Bergamo, dispensed from the three banns **and** from the closed season of Lent, with witnesses from **Parenzo** and **Ližnjan** and none from the castle.* **(doc.)**

**Two things follow, and both are easy to get wrong.**

**·** *A register of parish A can be **the only record of an event in parish B**. Searching Poreč's own books for this marriage would find nothing; it is filed at Svetvinčenat because that is where the couple belonged, not where they stood.*
**·** *The converse trap is worse: **do not read the parish as the place**. An archive that maps every act to its register's parish will put this couple at Svetvinčenat on a day they were thirty kilometres away.*

**The register usually says so plainly, in the clause nobody reads** — *the one between the dispensation and the witnesses, naming the church.* **It is worth reading every time, and this archive now does.**

rows.lab: A name, a year and a camp are not an identification
rows.text:
**On 29 September this archive went looking for a man who died at Dachau, and Arolsen offered one who matched on everything it had asked about.**

*«**DEFRANCESCHI, ANTONIO — 31 January 1909 — prisoner 8165**.» The surname, the birth year, the camp system. **Three fields, all agreeing, and all of them fields this archive had chosen to search on.***

**He was a different man.** *The record was an **ITS cross-reference card**, pointing to a file under **DEFRANCESCO** — born at **Moncalvo in Piedmont**, died at Dachau on **7 February 1945**. The man being looked for was born at **Gologorica in Istria** and died on **15 July 1944**.*

**Two rules come out of it.**

**·** **Test on a field you did not search on.** *Surname, birth year and camp were the query; **birthplace and date of death were not**, and they are what settled it. A match that agrees only on what you asked is not evidence — **it is your own question handed back to you**.*
**·** **An index entry is not a document.** *The thing that matched was an archive's **name-authority card**, created to link two spellings. Following it to the file it pointed at took one click and reversed the answer.* **Read the document the index stands for before believing the index.**

**⚠ And the near-miss had a hook in it.** *The Arolsen man was committed by **Sipo Trieste** and recorded as «Italian, Yugoslavian» — Adriatic markers that made him feel right. **A detail that fits the story is the most expensive kind of coincidence**, because it buys the rest of the match. The birthplace was written four times; it governed.*

rows.lab: Grep the archive BEFORE the source, not after
rows.text:
**6 October 2026. Asked whether Gračišće could be reached on FamilySearch, this session went and checked — and the archive had answered it on 15 September**, in a row that walked all **3,488** collections, opened 44, and tested «Austria, Catholic Church Records» and «Hungary, Civil Registration» by name against a control. *Stronger work than the re-run, three weeks old, sitting in the same file the re-run was about to be written into.* **And the second row written that morning was worse**: it announced a FamilySearch waypoint for **Krbune** as a find. *The waypoint was already in* **six files** *— the worklist had carried it since 1 October.*

**The cost is not the wasted hour. It is that a re-run written up as a discovery makes the archive look like it is finding things it already knew**, *and the next person cannot tell which rows are new ground.* ***So: grep `searched.json`, `sources.json` and `worklist.json` for the source AND the place BEFORE opening anything — not before publishing, which is too late to save the work.*** **A re-run is still worth writing down** — *this one confirmed the September negative from a second dataset and added two parishes to the absent list — but it must be labelled a verification in its first sentence.* *[Verification is worth publishing; it is not discovery.](/searched/)*

rows.lab: The roster is where findings go to be forgotten
rows.text:
**6 October 2026. Walking the death register turned up two Defranceschi the archive had already documented — and in both cases the roster row had not been told.**

· **[Maximilianus](/person/maximilianus-josephus-de-franceschi-1813/)**, *dead at four in 1817:* `gologorica.json` *carried the death that morning; the roster row still read* «**no register has been read for this person here**» *with* `d: null`.
· **[Josephus](/person/josephus-defranceschi-1763/)**, *dead 1838:* *the line data carried* «born 4 March 1765», *documented, and explicitly noted it as a correction of* «about 1763» *— and the roster row still said* **1763**, *with an empty note.*

**Neither was caught by a check.** *[check-propagation](/method/) greps for* ***retired wording***; *these were not wrong sentences but* ***missing*** *ones, and a missing sentence matches no pattern.* *Both surfaced only because the walk re-opened the page and the roster was then read back against it.*

***So: when a finding is written into a topic file, open the person's roster row in the same breath and look at it.*** **A person page is the address a reader is sent to.** *If the finding is on the line page and not on the row, every link into that person still shows the old state —* *and the archive looks, from the one angle a reader actually uses, as though the work was never done.*

*Both rows needed re-declaration in `data/decisions.json`, and [the gate refused the first commit until it got one](/method/), which is the system working.*

rows.lab: Look at the frame either side before calling a page read
rows.text:
**This reel shoots some openings twice, and both pairs found so far had a DEFECTIVE first exposure.**

· *Pages 27–28 (1805):* **M01069241** *has a loose slip of paper lying across the page,* ***hiding seven entries***; **M01069242** *has it lifted away.*
· *Pages 81–82 (1845–46):* **M01069269** *is cropped at the left edge and* ***the month column is gone*** *— seven deaths dated «22, 4, 26, 8, 28, 12, 26» with no month;* **M01069270** *is framed wider and gives Martii, Augusti, 8bris, 9bris, Decembris.*

**Neither was detectable from the frame itself.** *The slip looks like part of the page; the crop looks like the page simply starting there.* *[Two automated attempts to find duplicates had already failed](/method/) — ink coverage and pixel difference both scored a known duplicate inside the range of ordinary consecutive pages.*

***So the rule is manual and cheap: before accepting a page as read, open the frame on either side of it.*** **Twice now that has been the difference between a page recorded as read and a page actually read.**

*⚠ It also means the coverage figure overstates: it counts* **frames cited**, *and a duplicate pair is one opening counted twice.*

rows.lab: A section key is an id too — check before you mint it
rows.text:
**6 October 2026. A new finding was written into `gologorica.json` under the key** `duplicates`. *The key was already taken, by [the 1836 collation certificate](/gologorica-line/) — and* `json.dump` ***silently replaced it***. *Six paragraphs and a plate, gone, on a finding that had itself only been recovered after the crop-truncation error.*

**Nothing in the gate could see it.** *The JSON stayed valid, the site built, the links resolved, and* `check-story` *counted the same* **number** *of findings — it does not know* ***which***. *It surfaced only because the next insert asserted its anchor occurred exactly once and that assertion failed.*

***This archive's rule that [person ids are minted once and frozen](/method/) applies to section keys as well.*** *They are published addresses: a reader scrolling the line page meets them in order, and a clobbered one is a deleted page with no 404 to show for it.*

**So: `assert key not in data` before writing a new block, and when a key must be reused, diff the old value first.**

rows.lab: A sentence about how a register NAMES people is a claim about every page of it
rows.text:
**6 October 2026. This archive published that a Defranceschi had married a Deprato — joining the two families it had spent weeks separating — on the premise that** «these registers enter a married woman under her **birth** surname». ***The premise was backwards. They use the husband's.*** *[The claim stood two hours](/corrections/).*

**What killed it was eight pages further on in the same book**: «Lambertina **Defranceschi**, civis», *who was [born* **Peschle***](/person/lambertina-defranceschi-peschle-1786/). **And the premise's own star witness said so all along** — «Catharina **DEPRATO** *nata Rovisi* … uxor Joh: Baptista» *— Deprato is the husband's family, Rovisi is hers.* ***That entry had been cited as evidence for the opposite, because it was read for its surnames and not for its grammar.***

***This archive has now made this mistake twice in one week.*** *[The first was a sentence about when the register stops writing Latin](/corrections/) — true of two folios, false by folio 98.* **Both are the same shape: a generalisation about a book's HABITS, drawn from a handful of pages, and published as if it had been tested across the volume.**

**So the rule.** *Before a claim of the form* «this register always does X», *find* **three** *instances where the answer is known from outside the register, and say which they are.* *Here the test was cheap and would have worked: two women in this very book have maiden names recorded elsewhere, and both are entered under their husbands'.*

*⚠ Note what did* **not** *catch it: nothing in the gate can test a premise about a register's habits. [It was caught by continuing to walk.](/searched/)*

rows.lab: A wrong decade with the right day is a typo, not a namesake
rows.text:
**6 October 2026. Two rows in this archive carried a death year decades out, and both had been diagnosed the same way:** «a gap this wide means one side is describing a different person's death — most often a namesake in the same parish». ***Neither was a namesake. Both were transcription slips, and the tell was sitting in the data all along.***

| | this archive had | the register gives |
|---|---|---|
| [Clementina](/person/clementina-maria-defranceschi-1822/) | **10 March** 1840 | **10 March** 1870 |
| [Josephus](/person/josephus-lambertus-defranceschi-1808/) | **22 December** 1857 | **22 December** 1878 |

***The day and the month were right in both.*** **A confusion of two people scatters all three fields; a slip that preserves «10 March» and «22 December» and moves only the decade is a keying error.** *And in both the register's age closed on the declared birth to the month, which a different person's death would not do.*

**So, before reaching for «two people of the same name»:** *check whether the* **day and month agree**. *If they do, the cheap explanation is a mis-keyed year, and the* **age at death** *will usually settle it against the known birth — no second person required.*

*⚠ Both rows had also written down the right remedy —* «this needs the burial register, not a judgement» *— and it worked exactly as written, three weeks and two weeks later respectively. [The lesson there is to work the worklist down](/worklist/): the wrong years were live on the site the whole time.*

rows.lab: A house number is an address, not a household
rows.text:
**6 October 2026. [The Gologorica death book's index](/gologorica-line/) gives at least six house numbers TWO households each** — *house* **6** *is both* «Deprato Leonardus» *and* «Sestan Vincent»; *house* **9** *is* «Berdar» *and* «Peer»; *and the same at* **48, 55, 84 and 98**.

**This archive had been using house numbers as if they identified families** — «casa 31», «casa 36», «house 7» — *and had [raised a worklist item](/worklist/) and [published a claim it then withdrew](/corrections/) over a Defranceschi dying in what it called* «the Deprato house».

***The house was also a Sestan house. Three families at one address across seventy years, and [house 28 held Palmano, Peer and Flegar across eighty](/gologorica-line/).***

**So: a house number locates a BUILDING at a MOMENT.** *To use one as evidence about a family it needs* **a date** *and, because [the village was renumbered about 1806](/gologorica-line/),* **a statement of which numbering it is in**. *Without both it is not a fact about anybody.*

*⚠ The sharpest case: the archive's* «casa 31», *from the 1780s baptisms, is* **old** *numbering — and the index's* «**Rabar** alias Tomelincich N. 31» *is* **new**. ***Same number, different buildings, and nothing may be carried between them.***

rows.lab: Ask whether the register says anything about itself before reporting a nil from it
rows.text:
**9 October 2026. The Gračišće baptism book of 1667–1745 tells the reader, on folio 134, that it is incomplete.** *At the visitation of* **18 July 1732** *the Vicar General wrote into the register that baptisms had been* «**omissa per negligentiam**» — *omitted through negligence* — *and ordered the ministers to recover them and write them in* «**nulla interposita mora**». *[The decree is transcribed and plated in full](/gologorica-line/).*

***This archive had read sixty leaves of that book toward a nil without ever asking whether the book had an opinion about its own completeness.***

**So, before a nil is reported from any volume:** *read the* **front matter, the flyleaves, the blank-looking leaves and anything in a hand that is not the usual one.* *Visitation decrees, a new priest's note on taking over, a later hand's* «nastavlja se», *an index that does not match the entries — these are the register testifying about itself, and they are* **`doc`** *of the strongest kind, because they come from the authority that could see the original.*

**A nil from a book certified incomplete is still worth publishing.** *It is just a different sentence:* **not** «no Defranceschi was baptised here», **but** «no Defranceschi baptism was written into this book» — *and the second is the only one the evidence will carry.*

*⚠ It also qualifies the inference built on top of the nil. [The direct-line page reasons from the absence of the surname as a parent](/direct-line/) to the family not having lived at Gračišće. That reasoning survives — five occurrences and no residence across seventy-eight years is a real pattern, and [the 1826 census says the same thing from the other side](/gologorica-line/) — but it now has to be stated as a pattern in the record rather than a fact about the town.*

rows.lab: A thing catalogued is not a thing examined — grep the source's own title card, not only the surname
rows.text:
**9 October 2026. This archive announced the discovery of two confirmation rolls it had catalogued nine days earlier** — *[the film's title card says* «MATIČNA KNJIGA **KRIZMANIH** 1690-1694»*, and the frame map had carried it since 30 September](/corrections/).*

**The existing rule is to grep before claiming a discovery:** *grep [sources](/sources/), [searched](/searched/) and [the roster](/who/) for* **the source and the name**. ***That rule would not have caught this***, *because the thing being claimed was not a person and not a document — it was* **a part of a volume**, *and the volume was already listed under its own shelfmark.*

**So the rule gains a clause.** *Before writing that any part of a source is* **unread, unexamined, unlisted or newly found**, *grep for:*

1. *the* **frame or page range**, *which this archive records in [frame maps](/parish-books/) and [reel tables](/gologorica-line/);*
2. *the source's own* **title card or shelfmark** — «SIGNATURA 3.1», «ZM34K-215», «MKR», «MKK», «KRIZMANIH»;
3. *the* **native-language name of the record type**, *because a catalogue written in Croatian will not match an English word:* «krizmani» *does not look like* «confirmations», *and that is exactly how nine days passed.*

***The distinction that makes this worth its own rule:*** *[the archive's six earlier self-duplications](/corrections/) were things it had* **found and forgotten**. *This was a thing it had* **catalogued and never opened**. **A catalogue entry is the easiest place in the world not to look, because reading it feels like knowing it** — *and an archive that files well will make this mistake more often than one that files badly, not less.*

*The finding itself survived intact: the rolls had genuinely never been read, and reading them produced a real nil. **What was false was the novelty, not the evidence** — which is the usual shape of this error and the reason it is worth publishing rather than quietly rewording.*

rows.lab: Read every column of a ruled register, not the one your question names
rows.text:
**9 October 2026. This archive read the** `Pater` **column of thirty-six frames of the Gračišće baptism register, found no Defranceschi, and published that the family was** «not established at Gračišće in the eighteenth century». ***The* `Patrini` *column of the same frames holds about twenty of them.*** *[Correction published.](/corrections/)*

**⚠ The worst part is that the archive had already written the warning down.** *[Its own search record says](/searched/):* «*the* **father** *column was read … a Defranceschi could stand as a mother's maiden name or* **a godparent** … ***«None seen in twelve frames» is the claim; «none exists» is not***». **A correctly stated limit is not a closed gap.** *It sat for two days while the conclusion built on it spread into four files and an errand.*

**So two rules, and the second is the one that was missing.**

1. *A ruled register is a* **set of columns**, *and a question phrased* «was he living here?» *names only one of them. The surname can be in* **Pater, Mater (as* olim*/*nata*), Patrini, Conditio** *— and in this book it was in the one nobody asked about.* ***Sweep the whole row.***
2. *⭐* **When a limit is written into the log, raise it as a row in the same breath.** *A* «⚠ Limits:» *paragraph is a note to a reader who may never come; a worklist row is a note to somebody who will.* ***This archive's log is full of honestly stated limits, and that honesty is worth nothing until each one becomes a task.***

**⭐ And the payoff for closing it was not a tidier nil — it was a better fact.** *The father-column nil still stands. Set beside the godparent column it now says something far stranger:* ***the Defranceschi were at Gračišće as* cives *from 1791 to 1808 and had not one child baptised there in eighteen years.*** *Present, wanted at the font, not breeding in the parish. [An absence became a household.](/gologorica-line/)*

rows.lab: Never write a /who/ slug from a name — link /person/<pid>/, which always exists
rows.text:
**9 October 2026. The gate failed with** «*no such page*» *for* `/who/anna-de-franceschi-nobilis-pisinensis/` *and* `/who/vincenca-defranceschi/` — *two slugs composed out of the people's names while writing the prose around them.* **This is now the fifth slug invented and caught by the gate in one session**; *the others were* `/library/`, `/registers/`, `/sovereignty/` *and* `/gazetteer/`, *whose real names are* [/the-library/](/the-library/), [/parish-books/](/parish-books/), [/timeline/](/timeline/) *and* [/places/](/places/).

**The rule, because the failure is always the same shape:** ***a URL is a fact about the site, not a guess from a name.***

**For a person, there is one form that cannot be wrong:** `/person/<pid>/`. *[It is generated for* ***every*** *row in the roster](/who/), by pid, so the moment a person exists the page exists.* **`/who/<slug>/` is a different thing** — *a* **name index** *that gathers everyone sharing a name, [built from each row's own* `who` *field](/who/), which a new row does not have unless it is given one.* ***Writing a* `/who/` *slug for a brand-new person asks for a page nothing has built.***

**So:** *link* `/person/<pid>/` *for an individual; link* `/who/<slug>/` ***only*** *by copying a* `who` *value that is already in the roster; and for any other page, [check the file list](/archive/) rather than reasoning from the page's title.*

*⚠ The same failure also tripped the* **kit** *check in the same run, which validates links too — so one invented slug reports as two red lines and looks like two problems.*

rows.lab: A correction is a claim. Verify it as hard as the thing it corrects — harder, because it feels careful
rows.text:
**9 October 2026.
