This archive published a correction today, and the correction was wrong.** *A fast pass re-read a godmother as* «**Catharina** Defranceschi» *where the first pass had* «Theresia», *announced the fix, and [built a finding on top of it](/corrections/) — a second woman of the name crossing between two parishes. **Re-cropped at twenty times with the mother's cell alongside for alignment, the word is «Theresia». The original reading was right all along.*** *In the same pass four entries were re-dated to the wrong year, and [an apparent «disorder» in the register was announced that turned out to be a misread page header](/corrections/).*

**⚠ EVERY EVIDENCE RULE IN THIS ARCHIVE WAS WRITTEN FOR FIRST READINGS.** *[A hand is only legible against itself](/method/). [Never read rank off an abbreviation without a second construction](/method/). [Crop past the cell, not to it](/method/). [Assert the new text is present after writing](/method/).* ***None of them says anything about the second reading***, *and the second reading is where this archive has now been wrong twice in one day.*

**The rule, and the reason it is not obvious:**

> **A correction is a claim like any other.** *It needs the same crop, the same magnification, the same second construction, the same* `doc`. ***It needs them more***, *because a correction arrives already wearing the clothes of care — it is the act of a session that is paying attention, and that feeling substitutes for the work.*

**In practice, before publishing any correction of a reading:**

1. *Crop the disputed word* **again**, *at the magnification the original reading did not have, with an adjacent cell in frame for alignment.*
2. *Say which reading the evidence supports* ***and what would change your mind***. *«The word is X» is weaker than «the word is X, because the ascender at position 4 is crossed, and Y has no letter there».*
3. *If the correction creates a new person, a new place or a new link —* ***stop and verify once more***. *[A correction that generates a finding is the most dangerous kind](/corrections/), because the finding makes it attractive.*
4. *Prefer* **«this reading is not settled»** *to a confident swap. [A negative or an open question costs the archive nothing](/open-questions/); a confident wrong correction costs it a published claim, the claim built on it, and the correction of the correction.*

rows.lab: Check the closing sentence against the search log — it is the least careful line and the most quotable
rows.text:
**9 October 2026. Three published errors in one day, and all three were the same shape.**

1. *[A correction that was itself a misreading](/corrections/) — «Catharina» for «Theresia», made at speed because correcting feels like the careful act.*
2. *[Confirmation rolls announced as something «nobody had counted»](/corrections/) that this archive had catalogued from the film's own title card nine days earlier.*
3. *[«Baptising their children somewhere else, and the somewhere else is Gologorica»](/corrections/) — asserted about a book whose search row, four files away, says* «No Defranceschi baptism between 1799 and 1806».

**⚠ None of them was in the evidence. Every one was in the sentence that ties the finding off.**

*The body of a finding gets the crops, the magnification, the second construction, the* `doc` *tag. **Then comes the closing line — the one that says what it all means, the one a reader will quote** — and it is written from momentum, out of what the archive «obviously» holds, at the end of an hour's work when the hard part feels done.*

> ***It is also the only line most readers will carry away.***

**So, before publishing any finding, take its last sentence on its own and ask of it the three questions the body already answered:**

1. *Which* **file and row** *says this? Not «the archive holds» — which search key, which frame?*
2. *Is it* `doc`, `inf` *or memory? **If it names another source as agreeing, open that source.***
3. *Would it survive if the reader checked only this sentence?* *[A finding is told when a reader reads it](/method/) — and the closing line is what they read.*

*⚠ The pattern is not carelessness about evidence. It is **carefulness that stops one sentence early**, and it will recur unless the last line is treated as a claim rather than a summary.*

rows.lab: A told finding is not a drawn conclusion — re-read your own pages when a new question arrives
rows.text:
**9 October 2026. This archive spent a day establishing that the Defranceschi baptised no children anywhere for twelve years, listed three possible reasons, and then found the answer sitting on its own page, published five days earlier.**

*[«House 36, in eighteen months»](/gologorica-line/) was written on 6 October. It has the baby dead at six months in July 1791, the unmarried aunt dead of* «febris putrida» *in April 1792, the twenty-six-year-old wife dead of apoplexy four weeks after her — and the sentence* «**He did not remarry. He died a widower twenty-one years later.**» ***Everything needed to answer a question nobody had yet asked.***

**⚠ This is not the archive's usual failure and it should not be filed as one.** *[The standing rule is that a finding is done when it is TOLD, not when it is logged](/method/) — and this finding* **was** *told, in full, on the right page, with its plate and its sources.* ***What was not done was to draw its consequence when a new question made one available.***

> **A told finding is inert until somebody asks it a question it can answer.**

**So the rule has a second half:**

1. *When a new question is framed —* «where were the children?», «when did they arrive?» — ***grep the archive's own STORY pages for the years involved***, *not only its search log and its roster. The search log records what was looked for; the story pages record what was found, and a thing found for one reason answers another.*
2. *⭐ **Search by DATE RANGE, not by subject.** The house-36 block never mentions childbearing, fertility or a gap. It would not have matched any search for the question it answers. It matches* **1791–1792**, *and the question was about 1791–1803.*
3. *When the answer does turn up this way,* ***say that it was already there***. *[The temptation is to present a connection as a discovery](/corrections/), and the difference is the whole of this archive's credibility.*

close: None of this is a complaint about the sources. FamilySearch's films are the reason any of this was possible at all, and the volunteers who indexed the baptisms saved months. The point is narrower: **these tools answer the question you actually asked**, which is often not the question you meant — and the only defence is to open the image.
